sysadmin_function.title: Sysadmin 1 — The Sysadmin Function & the System Landscape
sysadmin_function.desc: The foundation of the system administration certification: the platform custodian thesis and the least-privilege paradox, the system's anatomy and document model, the managed-hosting boundary map, the admin's place as a hat at trade scale, the site configuration as the constitution beneath the constitutions, the daily posture and request channel, and the site book as the documentation spine.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The seventh certification: the platform custodian
lessons.html:
Six tracks certified the FUNCTIONS — the counter, the gate, the warehouse, the books, the people, the pay. This track certifies the FLOOR they all stand on: the system itself — and the person who keeps it: the system administrator. The thesis that opens the seventh certification: the system has a custodian — or it has a thousand casual owners, which is the same as having none.

Why the platform needs its own certification. The argument, made from six tracks' evidence: every discipline this academy taught RUNS ON the system — the documents live in it, the permissions fence it, the masters govern through it, the calendars fire from it — and every track's structural module ended by leaning on capabilities this track owns: the permission walks (logged in AS the roles — who builds those roles?), the settings constitutions (who holds the settings pen?), the reminder engines TESTED (who tests them?), the archives forever (who verifies the backups those archives depend on?). The functional tracks assumed a competent platform layer the way a building assumes its foundation — and in the trade's reality, that assumption fails constantly: the site where everyone is an administrator, the password shared on the counter's sticky note, the backup nobody has ever restored, the customisation nobody remembers making — the diseases are the SAME diseases six tracks fought (memory over documents, improvisation over masters, heroics over rhythms), living one layer down, undermining everything built above.

The custodian frame. The role's character, set before its duties: the sysadmin is a CUSTODIAN, not an owner — the functions own their data (the selling documents belong to the selling function, the pay masters to payroll's narrow pens: six tracks assigned every document an owner, and the admin is on none of those lists), and the admin custodians the PLATFORM those owners work on: the accounts that let them in, the permissions that fence them, the configuration that shapes their screens, the backups that guarantee their history, the health that keeps their mornings boring. The distinction is load-bearing and this track will enforce it repeatedly: the admin who reads the pay data because they CAN is the custody breach of the payroll track's tightest tier — the admin's power is access to everything, and the admin's governance (module 8) is therefore the strictest in the firm: maximum capability, minimum entitlement — the least-privilege paradox this track exists to resolve properly.

The track's map. This module — the function and the landscape (the system's anatomy, the managed boundary, the admin's place, the documentation spine). Module 2 — the deep module: users, roles, and permissions at full depth (the layer every prior track's permission walk pointed at, finally opened). Module 3 — master data governance and imports. Module 4 — backups, recovery, and continuity. Module 5 — updates, changes, and the test discipline. Module 6 — printing, email, and integrations. Module 7 — monitoring and the health reads. Module 8 — security, audit, and the structural layer that closes the track. The laws will arc from the system has a custodian to administration lives in structure — and HealthTrade's case continues: the firm that built six functions on its platform now formally staffs the platform itself.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The system's anatomy: the vocabulary
lessons.html:
Before duties, the map: what the system actually IS — its layers, named precisely, because the admin who cannot name the layers cannot reason about them. The anatomy chapter.

The site. The firm's tenancy: the SITE is the firm's complete, isolated instance — its database, its files, its users, its configuration, living at its address (the firm's own subdomain) — and the first vocabulary distinction the admin internalises: the site is the FIRM'S world (everything in it belongs to the firm's story), while the platform hosting it serves many worlds (the multi-tenant reality Chapter 3's boundary maps). One firm, one site, one story — and everything this track governs lives inside it.

The document model. The system's deepest idea, taught once and used forever: everything is a DOCUMENT of a TYPE — the doctype defines the shape (the fields, their kinds, the rules), the document is one instance of it (this invoice, this employee, this warehouse), and the six tracks' whole world resolves into this vocabulary: the masters are documents (the item, the customer, the salary structure), the transactions are documents (the invoice, the payment, the payroll run), the configuration is documents (the settings pages themselves), and even the fences are documents (the roles, the permission rules — module 2's terrain, stored in the same model it governs). The model's practical consequences for the admin: every document has an IDENTITY (its name — the naming series of six tracks' registrar laws, administered in module 3), a HISTORY (the versions and the trail — module 8's audit layer, on by design for what matters), a STATE (draft, submitted, cancelled — the lifecycle the functional tracks ride: the sealed run and the frozen close are this machinery), and an OWNER-and-permissions context (module 2). The admin who holds this model can reason about anything in the system from first principles — which is why it is Chapter 2 and not an appendix.

The layers beneath. The stack, at admin altitude: the DATABASE (every document's home — the single source the whole academy's one-version laws physically rest on: when six tracks said 'one version', they meant this layer's one row), the FILES layer (the attachments — the signed contracts, the scanned receipts, the payslip PDFs: documents' companions, backed up as deliberately as the database, because the invoice without its signed delivery note is half an evidence file), the APPS layer (the platform's capabilities and the firm's customisations — module 5's change discipline lives here), and the ACCOUNTS layer (the users — the humans' representations, module 2's raw material). The admin's mental model of any incident starts by placing it in a layer — the report that won't load (app layer? data volume?), the attachment missing (files layer), the login failing (accounts layer) — the triage instinct this vocabulary buys being the difference between a diagnostic and a panic.

The environments. The last vocabulary pair: PRODUCTION (the live site — the firm's actual world, where every change is real) and the TEST site (the copy where changes rehearse — module 5's whole discipline previewed in one distinction), with the admin's iron habit stated now and enforced later: nothing is tried for the first time in production — the sentence that separates administration from gambling, and the cheapest sentence in this track.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The managed boundary: who owns what
lessons.html:
The firm's system runs on managed hosting — and the single most important page in the admin's book is the BOUNDARY MAP: what the HOST owns versus what the SITE ADMIN owns. The boundary chapter — the track's equivalent of the adviser boundary, and just as load-bearing.

The host's side. What managed hosting owns and delivers, named so the admin neither duplicates nor neglects it: the SERVERS and infrastructure (the hardware, the operating layer, the network — invisible to the site admin by design), the PLATFORM's core software and its updates (the framework and application versions maintained, patched, and upgraded by the host on its announced cycle — module 5 governs the admin's side of that cycle), the INFRASTRUCTURE-level protections (the perimeter security, the encryption in transit, the platform monitoring), the infrastructure BACKUP machinery (the automated backup cycles running at platform level — with module 4 teaching the critical nuance: the host runs the machinery, the admin VERIFIES the firm's recoverability, because 'the host has backups' and 'we have tested that we can recover' are different sentences), and UPTIME (the availability commitment the hosting relationship states).

The site admin's side. What no host can own, because it is the firm's own governance: the USERS and their lifecycle (who has an account, joined to the HR track's events — module 2), the PERMISSIONS (who sees and does what — the fences are the firm's policy, expressed in configuration), the MASTERS' governance (the naming, the imports, the hygiene — module 3, joining six tracks' master laws), the CONFIGURATION (the settings constitutions of every track — the admin holds the pens' custody), the firm's DATA quality and evidence files, the CUSTOMISATION decisions (what the firm changes about its own site — module 5), the integrations' firm-side credentials (module 6), and the firm's CONTINUITY plan (module 4 — the host recovers infrastructure; the firm plans its own business continuity). The boundary's one-line summary for the site book's first page: the host keeps the system running; the admin keeps the firm governed on it.

The escalation channel. The boundary's working interface: the SUPPORT relationship, governed like every channel this academy has built — issues raised through the standing channel (the ticket, not the midnight call to a personal number — the one-channel law arriving at the hosting relationship), with the firm's side disciplined (the ticket that states the symptom, the steps to reproduce, the affected users, and the business impact is answered in one round; the ticket that says 'system not working' is answered with questions — the admin's ticket hygiene being the firm's own support-speed lever), SEVERITY used honestly (the everything-is-critical firm teaches the host's queue to discount it — the boy-who-cried-wolf economics of severity levels, stated plainly), and the escalation path documented in the site book (who to contact, through what, with what expectations — tested before it is needed, like everything in this academy).

The boundary's discipline. The chapter's closing rule, in the settled grammar: the admin never reaches ACROSS the boundary (the server-side question is a ticket, not an adventure; the platform update is the host's act, received per module 5's discipline) and never abandons their OWN side of it (the permission sprawl is not the host's problem; the untested restore is not covered by 'they have backups'; the sixty-day-stale user list is the firm's breach waiting) — the two failure modes being mirror images, and the boundary map on the wall being the cure for both: every incident, every question, every duty placed on its correct side in seconds, which is the map's entire job.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The admin's place: the hat, the paradox & the org
lessons.html:
Who the admin actually is at trade scale, the paradox their power creates, and where the role sits among six certified functions. The organisational chapter.

The hat, not the person. The scale honesty first, in the academy's standing tradition: at eleven people, the sysadmin is a HAT — a few hours a week worn by a capable operations person (HealthTrade's case: the ops lead), not a hired specialist — and the track is designed for exactly that wearer: every duty sized (the daily read is minutes; the monthly rituals an hour; the annual season some afternoons), every skill teachable (no code required for the site admin's whole scope), and the growth path real (the hat grows into a role as the firm grows into branches — the admin path beside the HR track's ladders). What the hat requires is not technical depth but the academy's own virtues: precision, rhythm, documentation, and the temperament to refuse corridor requests politely — which is why the best trade-scale admins are so often the same people who run good closes.

The least-privilege paradox. The role's central tension, named early because module 8 resolves it structurally: the admin holds the keys to everything — and must be the firm's LEAST casual user of them. The paradox's resolution, previewed: the admin's power is for PLATFORM acts (creating the account, building the role, restoring the backup), never for DATA acts (reading the pay figures because the fence is theirs to open, browsing the disciplinary file, 'checking' the sales numbers — each the custody breach of its track's tightest tier, committed by the person the fences trust most), with the enforcement structural where possible (the admin's own daily-work account distinct from the administrative account — the two-account discipline: the powerful account used deliberately, for administration, its sessions short and its acts logged; the daily account living under ordinary fences like everyone's) and cultural where it must be (module 8's conduct standard — the access log read by someone who is not the admin: nobody audits their own keys, the seventh telling of the academy's oldest separation).

The admin among the functions. The role's relationships, mapped: the admin SERVES the six functions (their requests for accounts, fences, formats, and fixes — Chapter 6's channel), CUSTODIANS what they share (the platform, the masters' machinery, the calendars' engine), and OWNS none of their data (the selling function's numbers are the selling function's; the admin's job is that the right people see them and nobody else does) — with the authority map explicit: functional configuration changes belong to the FUNCTION'S owner through the admin's hands (the payroll setting changes because payroll's configure authority decided, the admin executed, and both are named in the change log — the admin as the pen's custodian, never the decision's author), and the admin's OWN decisions confined to the platform layer (the session policy, the backup verification schedule, the update window: module 8 seats these formally).

The bottleneck warning. The chapter's closing pattern, familiar from six tracks and sharpest here: the FOUNDER-as-admin — the trade's default, where the owner holds the administrator password because the system arrived that way and nobody ever changed it — carrying every single-head disease at the platform layer (the founder's absence stalling every account request; the founder's casual omnipotence normalising exactly what module 8 forbids; the handover test failing before it is asked) plus one unique to this layer: the founder-admin cannot be fenced, so every tier this academy built — the payroll track's tightest, the HR track's sensitive — is one habit away from meaningless. The cure is this track's whole arc, and its first step is Chapter 8's case study: the hat formally assigned, to a named person, who is not the founder — the day the platform gets its custodian and the founder gets, at last, the same fences as everyone else, which six tracks have quietly been waiting for.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The site configuration: the constitution beneath the constitutions
lessons.html:
Every track walked a settings constitution; this chapter reveals what they stood on — the SITE-level configuration that shapes everyone's experience before any function configures anything. The seventh constitution, and the one beneath the other six.

The system settings walk. The site-wide fields, walked in the standing discipline: the LOCALE layer (the country, timezone, and language defaults — the timezone being quietly load-bearing: every timestamp in every trail this academy relies on renders through it, and the wrong timezone makes every 'when' in every dispute off by an hour), the FORMATS layer (the date format, the number format, the currency and its precision — the precision setting the ledger's kobo discipline physically rests on: Accounts 8's precision conviction has a field, and this is it), the SESSION layer (the login expiry, the concurrent-session posture, the password policy's strength — module 8's security constitution previewing its most consequential fields), the NAMING defaults (the series machinery module 3 administers — seated here), and the communication defaults (the notification and email switches module 6 governs — the flood-or-silence dial, set deliberately).

The settings custody, seventh telling. The academy's most-repeated law, at its deepest layer: every field above is a POLICY (the session expiry is a security policy; the precision is a financial policy; the timezone is an evidence policy), the pen is the NARROWEST in the firm (the site configuration changed by the admin, on a decision by the named authority, recorded in the change log — module 5's discipline receiving its first customers), and the corridor toggle convicted in its platform clothes — with the aggravating factor named honestly: a functional setting mis-toggled wounds its function, but a SITE setting mis-toggled wounds every function at once (the session expiry 'extended for convenience' weakening every tier's fences simultaneously; the precision nudged unbalancing reconciliation across two certified tracks) — the blast radius argument of the payroll track's pen tiers, applied to the layer where the radius is the whole site.

The configuration record. The chapter's deliverable, feeding Chapter 7's site book: every site-level setting recorded with its VALUE, its REASON, and its DECIDER (the one-page configuration record — written at implementation, updated by the change log, re-walked annually) — because the setting whose reason is forgotten is the setting someone will 'fix' (the timezone changed by a helpful hand who thought it looked wrong; the format 'corrected' to a preference — the undocumented configuration inviting exactly the casual edits its documentation would have refused), and because the record is the new admin's first hour of orientation (module 8's handover test, being fed from its first module — the pattern six tracks have proven: the documentation that is a byproduct of governing well IS the handover, and the site that is governed from a record survives its administrator by construction).

The defaults-are-decisions law. The chapter's closing conviction, stated for every implementation the certified admin will ever join: the site arrives with DEFAULTS, and every default kept is a decision made — the walk's job at implementation is to convert every consequential default from an accident into a choice (walked, decided, recorded — even when the decision is 'the default is right'), because the difference between the two is invisible for years and decisive in the one dispute, the one audit, the one recovery where the field turns out to matter — which is the settings-constitution argument all six tracks made, completed at the layer beneath them all.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The admin's posture: the reads & the request channel
lessons.html:
The admin's working rhythm — the daily glance that keeps mornings boring, and the channel that keeps requests governed. The posture chapter, previewing module 7's full machinery.

The daily glance. The reads, previewed at posture level (module 7 builds them fully): the ERROR log's morning scan (not read line by line — scanned for shape: the quiet log is the boring morning; the log that grew overnight is the day's first question), the BACKGROUND queue's health (the jobs that run the firm's automation — the reminders, the emails, the scheduled tasks: the stuck queue is every calendar's silent failure, and the glance catches it before the missed reminder becomes a lapsed licence), the LOGIN pattern's anomaly check (the failed-login cluster, the login at an odd hour from an odd place — module 8's security reads at glance depth), and the STORAGE trend (the site's growth watched monthly — the attachment habit that doubles the site in a year being a conversation, not a crisis, when read early). The glance's economics stated in the academy's cadence: five minutes daily against the alternative — the firm discovering its platform problems the way it once discovered stock problems, by collision.

The request channel. The one-channel law arriving at IT, and the discipline that saves every trade-scale admin: administration requests travel through the STANDING channel (the request document or ticket — the new account, the permission change, the format fix, the report question), never the corridor (the shoulder tap, the WhatsApp message, the founder's drive-by 'just quickly add...') — with the reasons the six tracks have made familiar: the corridor request is UNRECORDED (the permission granted with no trail is module 2's sprawl being manufactured in real time), UNPRIORITISED (the loudest request served first is the favour system running IT), and UNBOUNDED (the admin hat's few hours consumed by interrupts is the hat failing at its actual duties — the reads skipped, the backups unverified, the change log stale, all to answer taps). The channel's own governance: the request as a document (what, who, why, approved-by-whom where the request grants power — the permission request carrying its authoriser, because module 2's grants are events with authors), the SLA honest and published (the account request's turnaround stated; the emergency lane defined narrowly and honestly), and the queue read weekly for its shape (the clustering request is a training gap or a design gap — the request log as the platform's own query channel, read exactly as the payroll track read its pay queries: the channel measured by its own quieting).

The refusal craft. The posture's hardest skill, taught explicitly because the hat's wearer needs it scripted: the admin refuses REQUESTS, never people — the corridor ask met with the channel (log it and I'll have it done by tomorrow's SLA — the yes that preserves the system), the policy-breaking ask met with the policy and its owner (that fence is the payroll function's; if they authorise it through the request, I'll open it the same day — the admin as the pen's custodian, visibly not its author, which deflects the pressure to where the decision actually lives), and the founder's ask met identically (the moment Chapter 4 promised — the founder's request travelling the channel is the day the machinery becomes real for everyone watching, and the certified admin is prepared for it in advance, with the founder prepared too: the consultant's implementation includes exactly that conversation, before it is needed, which is this academy's signature move applied to its own administrator).

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The documentation spine: the site book
lessons.html:
The track's documentation layer, established in module 1 because every later module feeds it: the SITE BOOK — the one binder (physical or digital) that makes the platform legible to anyone who must hold it. The spine chapter.

The book's sections. The structure, laid down now and filled across eight modules: the boundary map (Chapter 3 — who owns what, the escalation path, the support contacts and expectations), the configuration record (Chapter 5 — every site setting with value, reason, decider), the access register (module 2's deliverable — every user, their roles, the grant events: the permission layer's memory), the master governance page (module 3 — the naming series, the import disciplines, the custodians per master), the continuity plan (module 4 — the backup verification log, the recovery runbook, the RPO/RTO decisions), the change log (module 5 — every customisation and configuration change: what, why, who decided, when, how reversed), the integration inventory (module 6 — every connection, its credentials' custody, its owner, its failure mode), and the calendar (module 8 — the admin's rhythms with names). Eight sections, eight modules — the book IS the track, materialised.

Documentation as byproduct, seventh telling. The academy's quiet thesis, at the layer where its violation is most expensive: nothing in the book is written FOR documentation — the boundary map is written to settle the first ownership confusion, the change log to make the first rollback possible, the access register to run the first permission walk — and the book assembles itself from governing well, which is why the undocumented site is not a documentation failure but a GOVERNANCE failure wearing one (the site with no change log is a site where changes were never governed; the missing access register is the sprawl's birth certificate), and why the consultant reads a prospect's site book — or its absence — as the single fastest health diagnostic the platform layer offers.

The book's readers. Who the spine serves, enumerated because each reader justifies it alone: the ADMIN themselves (the book is the working reference — the escalation path at midnight, the change log before every 'did we change something?'), the COVERAGE (the absence test's whole feasibility — the hat handed over for a holiday is the book handed over), the SUCCESSOR (module 8's handover test, passed or failed by this binder), the CONSULTANT (the implementation partner who can read the site's story instead of archaeologising it), the AUDITOR (the access register and change log being exactly what IT-adjacent audit asks for first), and the FIRM ITSELF in its hardest moments (the recovery runbook read during the incident it was written for — the site book being to the platform what the deceased-employee procedure was to the payroll track: the structure built in calm, carrying everyone when calm is gone).

The book's discipline. The maintenance rules, briefly: the book lives in a KNOWN place (and a copy lives outside the site it documents — the continuity plan that is only inside the system it recovers is a joke the incident will not find funny), its sections are OWNED (the admin owns most; the boundary map is co-owned with the host relationship; the integration inventory with each integration's function), it is UPDATED by events (the change that skips the log is module 5's conviction — the book fed by the rhythms, not by heroic annual rewrites), and it is WALKED annually (the book's own review on the calendar — stale documentation being worse than none, because it is believed). The chapter closes the module's foundations: the anatomy named, the boundary mapped, the hat assigned, the constitution recorded, the posture set, the spine established — and Chapter 8 watches HealthTrade do all of it in a quarter.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade appoints its custodian
lessons.html:
The platform gets its keeper. Every chapter clocks in.

The appointment (Ch. 1, 4). The trigger is honest and familiar: the MD — the site's only administrator since implementation — returns from the payroll track's absence-test triumph with the obvious question: every function now survives its people except the one they all run on. The hat is assigned deliberately: the operations lead (the HR track's developed deputy, the process temperament proven) takes system administration at four hours a week, with the appointment done as the academy does everything — a written scope (the site admin's side of the boundary map), a development plan (this track, module by module), and the two-account discipline from day one (her daily work account untouched; the administrative account created, powerful, logged, and used deliberately). The founder's own administrator access is retired the same week — the MD's note in the site book's first page is the chapter's thesis from the horse's mouth: I have been the least governed user of the most sensitive system in the firm. That ends with this appointment.

The boundary and the book (Ch. 3, 7). The first month is the map: the boundary session with the hosting relationship (the two-column page drawn — what the host owns, what HealthTrade owns; the escalation path documented and TESTED with a low-severity ticket, whose two-round resolution also teaches ticket hygiene by experience: the second ticket, written to the taught format, resolves in one), and the site book opened with its eight sections — five of them thin placeholders awaiting their modules, three filled immediately: the boundary map, the configuration record (the settings walk below), and the change log (opened with entry #1: the founder-access retirement itself — the book's first entry being its own origin story).

The constitution walked (Ch. 5). The site settings walk with the MD and the accountant finds the expected archaeology: the timezone correct by luck (never checked — now recorded as decided), the currency precision confirmed against the ledger's (the accountant's kobo conviction getting its platform verification), the session expiry found at a lax default from the implementation era ('convenient' — and weakening every fence six tracks built: tightened in the walk, announced per the standing discipline, the change log's entry #2), and every consequential default converted from accident to choice in one afternoon — the configuration record's first full page, signed and dated.

The posture lands (Ch. 6). The daily glance begins (five minutes with coffee — the error log's shape, the queue's health, the logins, the storage line), and the request channel opens with the announcement at the branch meetings: administration requests through the channel, the SLA published (accounts by next day, permission changes same-week with the owning function's authorisation, the emergency lane defined). The channel's first test arrives in week two, exactly as Chapter 6 predicted: the MD's corridor ask (just quickly give the new pharmacist access to the stock reports) — met with the prepared craft: log it with Inventory's authorisation and it's done within the hour. The request travels the channel; the fence's owner authorises; the grant lands with its trail — and the ops lead's note in the log is the module's whole posture in one line: said yes through the channel; the register never lied. The quarter closes with the glance boring, the queue quiet, the book growing by its own rhythms — and the platform, for the first time, a governed function among governed functions. The MD's quarter-note: the floor now has a keeper — and the keeper has a book.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the first law
lessons.html:
The platform layer's scar tissue — the diseases every site assessment finds first. Symptom → disease → fix.

Pattern 1 — the everyone-is-admin site. Symptom: five administrator accounts; fences that exist but exclude nobody who matters; every tier six tracks built, hollow. Disease: power granted for convenience and never reclaimed (Ch. 1, 4). Fix: one custodian, named; the administrator population reduced to the design; the two-account discipline; and module 2's full machinery to rebuild the fences meaningfully.

Pattern 2 — the founder-as-admin. Symptom: the owner holds the master password; every account request waits for them; every fence stops below them. Disease: the platform's single-head, unfenceable by definition (Ch. 4). Fix: the hat formally assigned to a named non-founder; the founder's access retired to an ordinary governed account; the day every tier becomes real.

Pattern 3 — the undocumented site. Symptom: nobody knows why any setting is set; changes leave no trace; the new admin archaeologises for months; the incident finds no runbook. Disease: governance never materialised (Ch. 5, 7) — the missing book being the missing governance's birth certificate. Fix: the site book's eight sections, fed as byproducts of governing well, walked annually, copied outside the site.

Pattern 4 — corridor IT. Symptom: requests by shoulder tap; permissions with no trail; the admin's hours consumed by interrupts; the loudest served first. Disease: the one-channel law never arrived at the platform (Ch. 6). Fix: the request channel with its SLA, the refusal craft scripted, the founder's requests travelling the same road — and the queue read for its shape.

Pattern 5 — the admin who owns data. Symptom: the admin 'checking' the numbers; the pay figures browsed because the fence is theirs; the tightest tiers meaningless above one login. Disease: custodian and owner confused (Ch. 1, 4). Fix: the least-privilege paradox resolved structurally — platform acts only, the two accounts, the access log read by another — maximum capability, minimum entitlement.

Pattern 6 — the boundary confusion. Symptom: the admin adventuring at the server layer, or neglecting their own side because 'the host handles it'; the untested restore covered by faith in someone else's machinery. Disease: the map never drawn (Ch. 3). Fix: the boundary map on the site book's first page — the host keeps the system running; the admin keeps the firm governed on it — every duty and every incident placed on its side in seconds.

The first law. The seventh track opens where the academy's grammar demands: the system has a custodian — a named keeper of the platform who owns none of its data, holds the narrowest pens beneath the other six constitutions, works through a channel, reads before being surprised, and writes the book that makes the floor survive its keeper. Six tracks built a firm that runs on documents; this track ensures the system holding those documents is governed by the same laws it enforces. Module 2 now opens the layer every permission walk pointed at: users, roles, and permissions — at full depth, ten chapters, the track's deep module.

users_permissions.title: Sysadmin 2 — Users, Roles & Permissions
users_permissions.desc: The track's deep module: the permission layer as policy-made-physics — the user lifecycle by events, roles mirroring functions, profiles and the grant discipline with the certification gate, doctype permissions and field-level permission levels, user permissions for territorial fencing, the systematic debugging method, and the annual permission walk mechanised.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The permission layer: policy as configuration
lessons.html:
Six tracks designed tiers — the payroll track's tightest, the HR track's sensitive, the inventory track's territorial fences, the accounts track's separated pens — and every one of them ended with the same instruction: the permission walk, logged in as the roles. This module opens the layer they were all pointing at: the PERMISSION machinery itself — and its thesis is the track's second law forming: access is least-privilege, granted by events, and walked annually.

Policy as configuration. The frame that governs the whole module: the permission layer is the firm's POLICY, expressed in configuration — who may see the pay figures is a payroll policy; who may adjust stock is an inventory policy; who may release payments is a treasury policy — and the machinery this module teaches is how those policies become PHYSICS instead of memos (the memo says the manager shouldn't see salaries; the permission level makes the field not exist on their screen — the difference between a rule and a fence being that the fence works at 2 a.m. on a bad day with nobody watching, which is the entire argument for configuration over culture that six tracks made and this module mechanises).

Least privilege, defined operationally. The principle stated as a working test, not a slogan: every user holds exactly the access their CURRENT duties require — no more (the sprawl this module hunts), no less (the over-fenced user working around the system is a different disease with the same cure: the fence sized to the duty) — with the test being answerable: for any user and any capability, the question which duty requires this? has a named answer, or the capability comes off. The principle's quiet corollary, stated for every implementation: least privilege is a MAINTENANCE discipline, not a design event — the fences drift as duties change (the promotion that adds without removing, the cover that never ends — the HR track's lifecycle events each carrying a permission consequence this module wires), which is why the law's third clause is walked annually and not designed once.

The module's map. Ten chapters, the track's deep module: the user lifecycle — accounts born and retired by events (2); roles — the vocabulary of capability (3); role profiles and the grant discipline (4); doctype permissions and permission levels — the fence anatomy, including the field-level machinery the pay tiers run on (5); user permissions — the record-level fences of the branch designs (6); the debugging method (7); the permission walk mechanised (8); HealthTrade's permission rebuild (9); and the patterns and the law (10). Throughout, one voice discipline: this module is written for the ADMIN as the machinery's custodian — the tiers' CONTENT was designed by six tracks' function owners, and the admin builds, maintains, and audits what those owners decided, which is Chapter 4 of module 1's authority map, now operating at the layer where it matters most.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The user lifecycle: accounts by events
lessons.html:
Before roles and fences, the accounts themselves — born, changed, and retired by the events that own them. The lifecycle chapter.

The account's birth. The user account created from the HR track's JOINER package (the day-one readiness discipline of HR 2, delivered at this desk: the account requested through the channel by the onboarding checklist, created before the start date, granted its role profile per Chapter 4 — the new hire arriving to a working login being the platform's contribution to the first-day experience the HR track designed), with the account's anatomy governed at creation: the IDENTITY (the email address as the username — the firm-domain address, not the personal one: the account on a personal email is an account the firm does not control at separation), the USER TYPE decided deliberately (the full system user for staff who work IN the system versus the portal-class user for those who only interact with their own slice — the distinction carrying licence and cost implications the admin tracks, because the firm paying full-seat costs for view-only needs bought the wrong tier by default), and the WELCOME flow governed (the first login, the forced password set, the orientation — the account handed over properly, not emailed as a password in plain text to be forwarded around).

The account's life. The changes, each by its event: the ROLE changes with the duties (the promotion's grant-and-review of HR 7 — executed here as Chapter 4's events), the NAME and detail changes maintained (the marriage-name change, the branch transfer's context — the record current because the account is a master like any other), and the DORMANCY watched (the account unused for the policy's horizon flagged monthly — the dormant account being either a person who left informally, a duty that evaporated, or a ghost's nest: all three worth finding, and the dormant-account scan being the lifecycle's cheapest read).

The account's retirement. The separation checklist's platform line, delivered: the account DISABLED on the last working day (HR 7's join map reversed — the departed with live logins being the security failure every audit finds first, and this desk being where that line is actually executed: the separation package's date arriving through the channel, the disabling scheduled, done, and confirmed back to the checklist's owner), with the retirement's disciplines: DISABLED, not deleted (the account's history is the firm's history — the documents owned, the actions logged: the deleted user punches holes in every trail six tracks rely on; the disabled user keeps the story intact while closing the door), the handover of ownership where workflows route to the person (the approvals re-pointed per HR 7's checklist — the workflow routing to a disabled account is the process stalled at an empty desk), and the shared-anything rotated (the integration credential or shared mailbox the person knew — module 6's custody, triggered by this event).

The lifecycle's register. The chapter's deliverable into the site book: the ACCESS REGISTER's first columns — every account, its holder, its type, its creation event, its status, its last-review date — the platform's mirror of HR 1's employee register, maintained by the same law (written by events, read monthly, reconciled at the walk), and the two registers RECONCILED as a standing read (every active account maps to an active employee or a documented exception — the service account, the auditor's temporary access — and every active employee who needs an account has exactly one: the reconciliation that makes ghosts structurally homeless at the platform layer, completing the cross-check the payroll track's controls began).

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Roles: the vocabulary of capability
lessons.html:
The permission layer's first building block: the ROLE — a named bundle of capability — and the design discipline that keeps the vocabulary clean. The roles chapter.

What a role is. The mechanics first: a role is a NAME that permission rules attach to (Chapter 5's rules say 'this role may read this doctype, write that one, submit the other') and users hold (the user with the role inherits its rules — capability by membership, not by individual grant), which makes the role the layer's unit of DESIGN: the firm's access policy is written in roles, and the quality of the role vocabulary determines whether the layer is legible or archaeological.

The design law: roles mirror functions, not individuals. The chapter's central discipline: roles are named for FUNCTIONS and duties (the till operator, the storekeeper, the payroll officer, the branch manager — the org design of six tracks, spoken as capability), NEVER for people (the role named 'Blessing's Access' is the sprawl's seed — unreviewable because its logic is a person's history, unreusable because the next hire isn't Blessing, and immortal because nobody remembers what it was for: the role-per-person site being the permission layer's version of the salary-structure-per-person disease the payroll track convicted, and cured identically — the vocabulary collapsed to the function count), with the granularity judged by the same test the payroll track used for components: a role exists because a CLASS of duty exists (the trade-scale firm needing perhaps a dozen roles — one per function-shape, not one per anxiety), and the standard roles the platform ships weighed before custom ones are coined (the shipped role that fits is free forever; the custom role is owned forever — the make-versus-take discipline at the vocabulary layer).

The role catalogue. The design's documentation, into the site book: every role listed with its PURPOSE (the duty-class it serves, in one sentence), its HOLDERS (maintained by Chapter 4's events), its permission summary (what it can broadly do — the detail living in Chapter 5's rules, the summary living here for the walk's reading), and its OWNER (the function whose policy it expresses — the payroll officer role owned by payroll's configure authority, the storekeeper role by inventory's: the admin custodians the catalogue; the functions own their entries — module 1's authority map at the vocabulary layer), with the catalogue's hygiene rules: no role without a purpose sentence (the role that cannot be described cannot be audited), no duplicate-purpose roles (the two roles doing one job are a merge waiting — the deduplication instinct of the master tracks), and the catalogue reviewed at the annual walk (the role nobody holds and nobody can explain is retired, not kept 'just in case' — the museum-of-old-deals conviction, at the role list).

The dangerous roles, named. The chapter's closing register: the roles whose grant is a different class of event — the SYSTEM-level roles (the administrative capability itself — held by the custodian per module 1's design, and by as close to nobody else as the firm can manage), the CONFIGURE-class roles (the settings pens of six constitutions — each held by its function's named authority, per the narrowest-pen tiers), and the OVERRIDE-class capabilities (the cancel-and-amend rights on sealed documents, the delete rights anywhere — Chapter 5 details them; this register names them so the grant discipline of Chapter 4 can treat them as what they are: the keys whose casual grant undoes six tracks of sealed-document law in one checkbox). The vocabulary chapter's one-line summary: few roles, function-named, purpose-sentenced, owner-assigned — the permission layer that can be read aloud is the permission layer that can be governed.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Role profiles & the grant discipline
lessons.html:
Roles bundle capability; PROFILES bundle roles into job-shapes; and the GRANT discipline governs how any of it reaches a human. The assignment chapter.

Role profiles: the job-shaped bundle. The mechanics and the design: the role profile is a named SET of roles matching a job (the 'Branch Storekeeper' profile carrying the storekeeper role, the basic-employee role, the branch-reporting role — one assignment, the whole shape), mapped from the HR track's architecture (the designations and grades of HR 1 each implying a profile — the org chart and the access chart being one design read twice, which is why the certified admin builds profiles FROM the HR track's structure rather than inventing a parallel one), and paying the standard-template dividends: the new hire granted their whole shape in one governed act (day-one readiness, mechanised), the job's access reviewed as a unit (the profile audited once serves every holder), and the drift made visible (the user whose roles differ from their profile is a DELTA with a story — the deliberate exception documented, or the sprawl surfaced: the profile turning the walk's hardest question, 'is this user's access right?', into a diff).

Grants as events. The discipline that keeps the layer's history readable: every grant and revocation is an EVENT with an author — the request through module 1's channel (what access, for whom), the AUTHORISATION by the fence's owner (the role's owning function saying yes — the admin executes; the owner decides: the payroll-role grant authorised by payroll's authority, never by the admin's judgment or the requester's insistence), the execution logged (who granted, when, on whose authority — the access register's event columns), and the TEMPORARY grant carrying its end date at birth (the audit-season access, the maternity cover — expiry-tracked like every temporary thing in this academy, because the cover that never ends is the sprawl's commonest species and the HR track's acting-role law has a platform twin).

The certification gate, wired. The join this academy promised in the HR track, delivered at this desk: HR 6's law — authority follows certification — becomes CONFIGURATION where the firm adopts it: the role grant gated on the certified capability (the till-supervisor role granted when the register shows the certification held; the payment-release seat granted against the treasury training's record), with the wiring honest about its mechanics (at trade scale this is a CHECKLIST discipline — the grant request's form asking for the certification reference, the admin verifying against the register before executing — and at platform maturity it can be automation; both count, because the gate's value is the check, not its plumbing), and the revocation mirror stated: the lapsed licence or expired certification of HR 1's worklist carries a permission consequence (the pharmacist role resting while the licence renews — the regulated trade's compliance, expressed as a fence).

The grant anti-patterns. The chapter's conviction list, brief and specific: the SELF-GRANT (the admin adding roles to their own account — module 8's conduct standard previewed: the admin's own access changes are authorised and executed by another, because nobody grants their own keys), the INSISTENCE-GRANT (the loud requester served without the owner's authorisation — the favour system at the fence line, and the refusal craft of module 1 pointed at exactly this), the CONVENIENCE-GRANT (the everything-role handed out to end a support conversation — the sprawl's express lane), and the UNREVOKED grant (the temporary that quietly became permanent — hunted by Chapter 8's walk, prevented by the end-date-at-birth rule). The chapter's summary for the site book: profiles from the org design, grants by authorised events, temporaries with end dates, and nobody — nobody — granting their own.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Doctype permissions: the fence anatomy
lessons.html:
The rules themselves: what a role may DO to a document type — the fence anatomy, right by right, with the field-level machinery the tightest tiers run on. The rules chapter.

The permission rule. The unit: role × doctype × RIGHTS — the rule saying this role, on this document type, holds these specific capabilities: READ (see it exists and open it), WRITE (change drafts), CREATE (make new ones), SUBMIT (seal — the right that fires the frozen-document machinery six tracks rely on), CANCEL and AMEND (unseal and revise — the override-class keys of Chapter 3's register: the cancel right on a sealed invoice is the power to unwind the counter's history, granted accordingly), DELETE (remove — the right this academy grants almost nowhere, because the trail-punching delete is the enemy of every evidence law), and the access rights beyond (REPORT — the query and report surfaces; EXPORT — the data-leaves-the-building right, held as narrowly as the payroll track's tightest tier demanded; SHARE — Chapter 7's governed exception; PRINT and EMAIL — the document's outbound doors). The design discipline: rights granted individually and deliberately per role per doctype (the read-only role that can somehow export the full customer book was granted by checkbox momentum, not decision — every ticked box a policy, in the settings-constitution grammar).

Permission levels: the field-level fence. The machinery the pay tiers physically run on, taught carefully because it is the module's most consequential subtlety: fields on a doctype carry LEVELS (level 0 the default body; levels 1, 2, and beyond the sensitive strata), and permission rules grant rights PER LEVEL — so the employee doctype's identity fields sit at level 0 (readable by the roles that need the person), while the pay-relevant and sensitive fields sit at a higher level readable only by the roles the tier design named (the payroll track's 'the band, not the figure' and the HR track's sensitive tier being, mechanically, THIS: the field's level plus the rule's level-grant — the manager opening the employee record and simply not seeing the salary field, because for their role it does not exist). The admin's craft with levels: the level map DOCUMENTED per sensitive doctype (which fields at which levels, readable by which roles — the site book's page the walk re-verifies), changes to levels treated as tier-design changes (the function owner's decision through the change discipline — a field's level moved is a policy moved), and the verification empirical always (logged in as the role, the record opened, the field absent — the fence proven, not assumed).

The if-owner nuance. The rule modifier worth its own paragraph: rights grantable IF-OWNER — the user holding them only on documents they created (the self-service patterns riding this: the employee reading their OWN leave applications and no one else's — the HR track's self tier, mechanised in one checkbox), with the nuance's edge taught: if-owner READ is the self-tier's engine, while if-owner WRITE on submitted-adjacent flows needs the workflow's scrutiny (the creator editing their own document after approval began is a process question the function owner answers, not a default).

The combination logic. How the pieces resolve, stated plainly because debugging depends on it: a user's effective capability is the UNION of their roles' grants (any role granting read grants read — which is why the everything-role poisons every other design: one over-broad role held silently defeats ten careful ones, the additive logic making sprawl a one-way ratchet that only the walk reverses), then FILTERED by the record-level fences (Chapter 6's user permissions — the role says 'may read invoices'; the user permission says 'only this branch's'), then modulated by the document's state and the workflow's rules (the submitted document refusing writes regardless of rights — the state machinery outranking enthusiasm). Union, filter, state — the three-word model that makes Chapter 7's debugging systematic instead of superstitious.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — User permissions: the record-level fence
lessons.html:
Roles answer WHAT a user may do; user permissions answer WHICH RECORDS they may do it to — the territorial layer the branch designs run on. The record-fence chapter.

The mechanism. The user permission: a per-user restriction binding them to specific records of a doctype — this user, the Company doctype, THIS company; this user, the Warehouse doctype, THESE warehouses; this user, the Branch or Cost Center, THIS branch — with the effect flowing through the links: the user fenced to the Ibadan branch sees Ibadan's documents wherever documents carry the branch link (the invoice list filtering itself, the stock report showing their warehouses, the employee list — where the design fences it — showing their people), the record-level fence riding the document model's link fields, which is why clean master design (module 3) is this fence's silent prerequisite: the territorial fence is only as good as the territory fields on the documents.

The strategic uses. Where the record fence earns its keep, mapped to six tracks' designs: the BRANCH isolation (the multi-branch firm's operators seeing their own world — the Ibadan till assistant with no window into Lagos's numbers: the need-to-know principle at geographic scale, and the design the Inventory and Selling tracks' territorial disciplines assumed), the WAREHOUSE custody fences (the storekeeper bound to their custody — Inventory's custodian law, expressed as configuration: the adjustment they can even attempt limited to the stock they answer for), the COMPANY boundary (the multi-entity firm's legal-person separation — Accounts 8's companies-by-law, fenced so the entities' books cannot cross-contaminate by accident), and the SELECTIVE openings (the supervisor fenced to two branches, the auditor's temporary window — the fence as scalpel, not just wall).

The traps. The record fence's failure modes, taught before the enthusiasm: the OVER-FENCE (the fence that breaks legitimate workflows — the head-office accountant fenced to one branch cannot run the consolidated close; the payroll seat fenced from a branch cannot pay it: the fence tested against the holder's ACTUAL duties, per the least-privilege test's both directions), the DEFAULT-VALUE tangle (the user permission that also drives defaulting — the fenced value auto-filling forms: useful when intended, mystifying when not, and the admin knows the difference), the APPLY-TO scope discipline (the restriction scoped to the doctypes it should govern, not blanket-applied — the fence on Company applied to everything strangling doctypes that legitimately cross companies), and the MISSING-LINK illusion (the fence that seems to work because the list happens to filter, while documents without the link field pass freely — the fence verified empirically per doctype, as the roles were: opened as the user, probed at the edges, proven).

The register's territorial page. The chapter's deliverable: the record-fence map into the site book — per fenced user or profile-class: WHAT they are bound to and WHY (the branch assignment from the HR record being the authorising fact — the fence maintained by the transfer event of HR 7: the person moved to Akure has their fence moved the same day, by the same event, or the platform contradicts the org chart), reviewed at the walk beside the roles — because the territorial layer drifts exactly as the capability layer does (the transfer that moved the person and not the fence; the two-branch exception that outlived its reason), and the walk that reads both layers against the HR track's current truth is the reconciliation that keeps the platform's map matching the firm's actual shape, which is the whole point of the layer this chapter closes.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The debugging method: systematic, not superstitious
lessons.html:
The admin's most frequent permission work is neither design nor audit — it is the COMPLAINT: I can't see X / why can she do Y? This chapter is the method that answers both in minutes. The diagnosis chapter.

The can't-see walk. The complaint resolved by walking Chapter 5's combination model in order — UNION, FILTER, STATE — as a checklist: 1, the user (account active? the right account? — the embarrassing first check that solves a surprising share), 2, the roles (does any held role grant the capability on the doctype? — the role list against the catalogue), 3, the rule's detail (the right itself granted? read but not report? report but not export? — the specific verb checked, because 'can't see' means five different rights in users' mouths), 4, the permission level (the field they miss sitting at a level their roles don't reach — the 'record opens but the field is blank' signature, diagnostic in one look), 5, the user permissions (the record fence excluding the records in question — the 'others see it, I don't' signature), 6, the sharing and workflow layer (the document in a state or a stage their rights don't reach), and the answer given by POINTING (the payroll track's answered-by-pointing, at the platform desk: the diagnosis shown, the fix named, and — critically — the fix routed: if the access SHOULD exist, the grant travels Chapter 4's event with its owner's authorisation; the debugging session never becomes a granting session, because diagnosis and authorisation are different powers and the admin holds only one of them).

The shouldn't-see inverse. The graver complaint, walked with the same model in reverse: why can this user do that? — the effective capability decomposed (which role grants it? the union's culprit found — usually the over-broad role of Chapter 5's warning, held from an old duty), the finding treated per its weight (the surprising capability is a walk-item at minimum and an incident at maximum — the user who could export the pay register is a finding with module 8's incident process behind it, not a quiet checkbox fix: the fence that was open gets closed AND the question 'was it used?' gets asked, with the logs answering), and the root cause fed back (the role redesigned, the grant discipline tightened — the debugging layer's findings being the walk's off-season intelligence).

Sharing: the governed exception. The mechanism that bypasses the fences by design, governed accordingly: document SHARING (the specific document opened to a specific user — the fence's deliberate, per-document exception: the one contract shared with the adviser's account, the one report with the auditor), legitimate exactly because it is SPECIFIC and visible (the share is a logged act on the document — auditable per document, unlike a role grant's broad sweep), and watched for its culture (the share-workaround pattern — the team routinely sharing documents to defeat a fence that blocks real work — being not a sharing problem but a DESIGN problem surfaced: the fence mis-sized, fixed at the design layer through the owner, the workaround retired: the clustering share read exactly as every clustering signal in this academy — the same lesson wearing platform clothes).

The test-site discipline. The method's laboratory: permission changes REHEARSED on the test site where the change is non-trivial (the level moved, the role redesigned — toggled and tested as the affected roles before production sees it: module 1's nothing-first-in-production, applied to the layer where a slip exposes pay data or strands a branch), and the empirical habit absolute: every fix VERIFIED as the affected user (logged in as the role, the capability confirmed present or absent — the fence proven, never assumed: the six-track canon's phrase, now revealed as this desk's daily method rather than an annual event).

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — The permission walk: the audit, mechanised
lessons.html:
Six tracks prescribed it; this chapter owns it: the ANNUAL PERMISSION WALK — the audit that proves the whole layer, mechanised into an afternoon. The walk chapter.

The walk's preparation. The desk work before the logins: the ACCESS REGISTER reconciled (every account against the HR track's active list — the leaver scan first, because the departed with live access is the walk's gravest possible find and the cheapest to check; every account's roles against its profile — the deltas listed, each needing its documented reason or its revocation), the ROLE CATALOGUE reviewed (every role's purpose sentence still true, its holders still needing it, the unheld and unexplainable retired), the TEMPORARY grants audited (every end date checked — the expired-but-active grant being the sprawl's freshest species), and the walk's TARGET LIST drawn (the sensitive surfaces six tracks named: the pay-bearing doctypes and their levels, the sensitive HR tier, the export rights everywhere, the override-class capabilities, the administrative population itself).

The walk proper: logged in as the roles. The canon, executed: a representative account per role-shape (the test users maintained for exactly this, or the walk performed beside the actual holders), and the surfaces walked EMPIRICALLY — the LIST VIEWS opened (the employee list's columns as the branch manager sees them — the birthday-leak find of the HR track's case being this exact check), the sensitive RECORDS opened (the pay fields absent for the roles the tier excludes — the level map proven), the REPORTS run (each people- and money-bearing report as its intended audience — the report that shows more than its viewer's fence is the layer's classic leak, because reports can travel paths list views don't), the EXPORTS attempted (the data-leaves-the-building right confirmed held only where the design says), and the TERRITORIAL fences probed (the Ibadan login shown only Ibadan — the edges tested, not the happy path: the unfenced doctype hunted per Chapter 6's missing-link trap).

The findings' discipline. The walk's output, governed: every find LOGGED (the walk's report into the site book — the find, its severity, its fix, its owner, its date), fixed through the CHANNELS (the revocation as an event like the grant was; the level change through the function owner; the design flaw through module 5's change discipline — the walk finds; the owners decide; the admin executes: the authority map holding even in audit season), the was-it-used question asked for the grave finds (the open fence's history read in the logs before it closes — the finding's severity being partly its exploitation), and the walk's METRICS trended year over year (the finds count falling as the grant discipline matures — the walk measured by its own quieting, the academy's standard success shape, at the layer that guards all the others).

The walk's calendar seat. The scheduling notes that make it real: ANNUAL as the floor (the standing walk on module 8's calendar), EVENT-TRIGGERED re-walks for the moments that concentrate risk (the org restructure, the system's major update, the admin handover — each a mini-walk of the affected surfaces), and the walk's ownership honest (the admin RUNS it; a second pair of eyes reviews the administrative population's own access — nobody walks their own keys, the module's conduct law applying to its audit: module 8 seats this formally, and the walk report's last page is always the admin's own access, reviewed and signed by someone else). The chapter's closing line, six tracks in the making: the permission walk is where the firm's every tier, fence, and pen is proven real — an afternoon a year, against the alternative of finding out in the leak.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Case study: HealthTrade's permission rebuild
lessons.html:
The layer, rebuilt from six tracks' designs. Every chapter clocks in.

The lifecycle wired (Ch. 2). The access register opens with the reconciliation — and finds the implementation era's residue: nineteen accounts for seventeen active staff (one leaver from before the HR track's checklist existed — disabled the same hour, the logs read: unused since departure, the finding closed clean; one duplicate from an email change — merged per module 3's discipline). The joiner and leaver events wire to the channel: the next hire's account exists on day minus-one; the next separation's disabling confirms back to the checklist within the hour. The dormant scan enters the monthly glance.

The vocabulary rebuilt (Ch. 3-4). The role audit finds the expected museum: fourteen roles for eleven people, three named after individuals ('Chidi Stock Access' among them — its purpose archaeologised, its capabilities absorbed into the storekeeper role, the museum exhibit closed), and one everything-role held by four people 'from the setup days' — the union-logic poison named at the whiteboard, the role retired, its holders re-granted their actual shapes. The rebuild lands at NINE function-named roles with purpose sentences and owners, bundled into six profiles mapped from the HR track's designations — and the grant discipline goes live with the certification gate as a checklist rule: the till-supervisor grant request now carries its certification reference, verified against the register before execution.

The tiers proven (Ch. 5). The level map is the rebuild's centrepiece: the employee doctype's pay-adjacent fields confirmed at their elevated level, the payroll doctypes' rules granted only to the payroll officer role and the approval seat — and the empirical verification delivers the module's signature moment: the branch manager's test login opens an employee record and the salary section simply is not there (the MD, watching: so the policy is now physics — the chapter's thesis, quoted back by its customer). One find at this layer: the export right on a stock report reachable by the till operator role (checkbox momentum from the setup era — revoked through Inventory's owner, the was-it-used logs read: never used, closed clean).

The territories fenced (Ch. 6-7). The branch fences land: Ibadan and Akure operators bound to their branches, warehouses fenced to their custodians, the head-office seats deliberately unfenced (the over-fence trap avoided by design — the accountant's consolidated duties named in the register as the reason). The first debugging case arrives on schedule: a new Akure hire can't see the stock report — the method walks it in four minutes (user active, roles right, rule grants report... the record fence missing: the account created before the branch assignment landed — the fence added by its event, the fix routed properly), and the case enters the site book as the method's worked example. One share-workaround read: three shares of the same price list to the same two users in a month — the design question surfaced (the fence mis-sized for a legitimate cross-branch duty), fixed at the design layer through Selling's owner, the workaround retired.

The first walk (Ch. 8). The annual walk runs in one afternoon: the register clean (the rebuild's dividend), the roles' catalogue true, two temporary grants found expired-but-active (the audit-season access from last year's statutory review — revoked, and the end-date-at-birth rule's enforcement tightened), the list views and reports walked as the roles (one report found showing unfenced branch columns — fixed through the owner), the admin's own access reviewed and signed by the MD (the last page's law, honoured from walk one). The walk report files as the site book's newest section — and the ops lead's closing note is the module in one line: the fences used to be what we believed; now they are what I proved on Tuesday.

lessons.title: Chapter 10 — Common mistakes & the second law
lessons.html:
The permission layer's scar tissue. Symptom → disease → fix.

Pattern 1 — role-per-person sprawl. Symptom: roles named after people; the vocabulary unreadable; every audit an archaeology. Disease: the design law inverted (Ch. 3). Fix: roles mirror functions — the catalogue collapsed to the function count, purpose-sentenced, owner-assigned, the personal roles absorbed and retired.

Pattern 2 — the everything-role. Symptom: one broad role defeating every careful design; capability nobody meant, held by half the firm. Disease: the union logic poisoned at its root (Ch. 5) — sprawl's express lane. Fix: the role retired, holders re-granted their actual shapes, and the walk's target list watching the broad grants forever.

Pattern 3 — the unused level. Symptom: sensitive fields at level 0; the pay figures visible to every role that can open the record; the tightest tier a memo. Disease: field-level fencing never deployed (Ch. 5). Fix: the level map per sensitive doctype, the rules granted per level, and the fence proven empirically — the policy made physics.

Pattern 4 — the share-workaround culture. Symptom: routine sharing defeating the fences; the exception become the method. Disease: a design problem wearing a sharing problem (Ch. 7). Fix: the clustering shares read as the signal they are — the fence re-sized through its owner, the workaround retired, sharing returned to its governed-exception role.

Pattern 5 — the walk never run. Symptom: fences believed, never proven; the leaver with live access; the maternity cover's residue immortal; the leak discovered by the leak. Disease: least privilege treated as a design event instead of a maintenance discipline (Ch. 1, 8). Fix: the annual walk on the calendar with its checklist, the event-triggered re-walks, and the metrics trended — an afternoon a year against finding out the hard way.

Pattern 6 — grants without events. Symptom: access with no trail; nobody knows who authorised what or why; the register that cannot be reconciled. Disease: the grant discipline absent (Ch. 4). Fix: grants as authorised events through the channel — the owner decides, the admin executes, the register remembers, temporaries expire — and nobody, ever, granting their own.

The second law. The custodian named; now the fences proven: access is least-privilege, granted by events, and walked annually — accounts born and retired by the lifecycle's events, roles mirroring functions in a catalogue that can be read aloud, profiles from the org design, rights and levels expressing each tier's policy as physics, territories fenced to the firm's actual shape, complaints diagnosed by method, and the whole layer proven empirically once a year by someone logged in as the roles. The permission layer is where six tracks' designs become real or stay memos — and the certified admin is the difference. Module 3 turns to the data the fences guard: master governance and the import machinery.
