changes_updates.title: Sysadmin 5 — Updates, Changes & the Test Discipline
changes_updates.desc: Every change staged, documented, reversible: the host's update stream received by ritual with the post-update walk, customisations gated by make-vs-take and owned forever, custom fields born with their permission levels, print formats that never contradict their sealed records, workflow edits as authority changes, and the one change ceremony with how-to-reverse in every log entry.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Every change is staged, documented, reversible
lessons.html:
The site the firm went live on is not the site it runs today, and never will be again: the platform updates beneath it, the firm customises above it, and the configurations drift with every governed decision. Change is the platform's only constant — and this module's thesis is the track's fifth law: every change is staged, documented, and reversible — or it is a gamble wearing a fix's name.

The two change streams. The module's map begins with the distinction that organises everything: changes arrive from TWO directions — the HOST'S stream (the platform updates the managed relationship applies on its announced cycle: not the firm's choice to receive, entirely the firm's duty to receive WELL — Chapter 2) and the FIRM'S stream (the customisations and configuration changes the firm chooses: the custom fields, the print formats, the workflows — Chapters 3-6, every one a decision the firm owns forever) — with both streams governed by ONE procedure (Chapter 7's ceremony), because the discipline that makes a change safe does not care who initiated it: the staging, the documentation, and the reversibility apply identically to the update the firm received and the field the firm added.

Why change is where sites die. The stakes, argued from the consultant's case files: the healthy site degrades through exactly two mechanisms, and both are change mechanisms — the DRIFT (the accumulated small changes nobody staged, logged, or can explain: the site three years on where every screen carries someone's forgotten improvisation, every report a mystery layer, and every new problem undebuggable because the baseline is unknown — the archaeology sites every consultant inherits, built one unlogged change at a time) and the BREAK (the single change that collided with something it never tested against: the update that shifted a report the pay run reads, the field that leaked through a permission level, the workflow edit that orphaned a live approval — each survivable when caught in staging and expensive when discovered by the counter). The cure for both is the same ceremony, and the ceremony's cost is minutes per change — which makes this module the academy's standing economics argument (the storm-into-weather trade) applied to the platform's own evolution.

The test site, promoted. Module 1 introduced the second environment and its iron habit; this module makes it the working instrument: the TEST SITE as the rehearsal stage for both streams (the update previewed where the boundary provides the preview; the customisation built and proven there first, always), refreshed on a rhythm (the test site that diverged from production two years ago rehearses nothing — the periodic refresh from a production backup being the drill of module 4 doing double duty: one restore, two purposes: recovery proven AND the stage re-set), and the habit's phrasing sharpened for this module's use: nothing reaches production that was not seen working somewhere else first — the sentence that governs every chapter that follows.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The update cycle: the host's stream, received governed
lessons.html:
The platform updates arrive on the host's cycle — the firm does not choose whether; it chooses HOW WELL. The receiving discipline. The updates chapter.

The cycle, known. The boundary's update facts documented in the site book: the host's update CADENCE (the routine maintenance rhythm, the major-version cycle — asked, answered, recorded), the ANNOUNCEMENT channel (where update notices arrive — subscribed, read, and routed: the update notice that lands in an unwatched inbox is the surprise the whole chapter exists to prevent), and the WINDOW conventions (when updates land — the timing the firm's own calendar reads: the major update scheduled against the firm's critical dates, because the platform upgrade on payroll-run week is a collision the calendar could have prevented, and the boundary conversation about timing is legitimate and expected — the managed relationship serves the firm's rhythm where it reasonably can, and the firm that never asks never benefits).

The release notes, read. The admin's first duty per update: the RELEASE NOTES read for the FIRM (not skimmed for interest — read against the firm's actual flows: what changes in the modules the firm uses, which behaviours move, what is deprecated that the firm touches — the reading being a triage: most notes affect nothing the firm does; the ones that do get flagged to the owning functions BEFORE the update lands, per the never-surprised law now applied to the functions themselves: the selling function told that the pricing behaviour changes beats the selling function discovering it mid-quote), and the customisation COLLISION check (Chapter 3's register consulted — the firm's custom fields and formats read against the update's touched areas: the customisation is maintenance debt, and update time is when the interest is paid).

The post-update walk. The chapter's core procedure: after every significant update, the firm's CRITICAL PATHS walked on production (the checklist maintained in the site book — the invoice created and printed, the payment entered, the stock movement posted, the payslip previewed, the key reports opened: fifteen minutes of deliberate walking, per the paths the firm actually lives on), the walk performed BEFORE the branches open where the window allows (the update landed overnight, the walk at dawn — the break caught by the admin's checklist instead of the till's queue), findings routed immediately (the shifted report to its owner, the broken format to Chapter 5's repair, the genuine regression to the boundary's ticket with module 1's hygiene: symptom, steps, impact), and the walk LOGGED (the update's entry in the change log — the version received, the walk's result, the findings: the update history being half the answer to every 'when did this start?' question the future will ask).

The preview discipline. Where the boundary provides pre-update access (the test site updated ahead, the staging preview): the preview USED (the walk run there first — the finding moved from production-morning to preview-week, which is the whole point of having one), and where it does not, the walk's promptness doing the work — with the chapter's honest closing note about the managed trade-off: the managed platform's updates are one of its greatest values (the security patches applied, the features arriving, the reform-resilience of the payroll track's configuration resting on a current platform) AND a standing change stream the firm must receive with discipline — the firm that resents updates has misunderstood the bargain; the firm that ignores them has misunderstood the risk; the certified admin does neither, and the receiving ritual above is what 'neither' looks like in practice.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Customisations: the make-vs-take discipline
lessons.html:
The firm's own change stream begins with a decision this chapter governs: whether to change the system at all. The make-vs-take chapter — the module's most valuable and least technical.

The customisation catalogue. The instruments, named for the chapters ahead: CUSTOM FIELDS (the doctype's shape extended — Chapter 4), PROPERTY changes (the existing field's behaviour adjusted — the label, the default, the mandatory flag), PRINT FORMATS (the documents' faces — Chapter 5), WORKFLOWS and automation rules (the process's shape — Chapter 6), CLIENT SCRIPTS and server logic (the behaviour layer — flagged here as the deepest end: legitimate, powerful, and carrying the highest ownership cost, engaged through the implementation partner's discipline rather than improvised), and CUSTOM DOCTYPES (whole new document types — the largest make, weighed accordingly). Every instrument shares one property the chapter exists to teach: a customisation is owned forever — it must survive every future update (the collision check of Chapter 2, paid at every cycle), be understood by every future admin (the documentation debt), and be maintained against every future change of the flows it touches (the field that feeds a report that feeds a decision — the dependency owned as long as any link in it lives).

The make-vs-take test. The decision procedure, run on every customisation request: first, does the standard way serve? (the platform's existing capability searched honestly — the request for a custom field that duplicates a standard one the requester never found being the commonest case, and the admin's product knowledge being the cheapest customisation-avoidance technology the firm owns), second, is the gap real or is it habit? (the request that recreates the old spreadsheet's shape inside the new system — the 'we've always had a column for...' request — tested against whether the firm USES the thing or merely inherited it: the migration's great opportunity being the shedding, not the reproduction, of the old system's accidents), third, is it a software gap or a process gap? (the request that patches a process problem with a field — the 'add a status field so we can track...' that is really an ungoverned flow wanting a workflow, or a discipline wanting a calendar line: routed to the owning function as the design signal it is, per the standing read), and only then, make — with the making sized (the smallest instrument that serves: the property change before the custom field, the custom field before the custom doctype) and the ownership priced aloud (the request's owner told what forever costs, because the function that wants the field maintains the reason it exists).

The customisation register. The catalogue's governance memory: every customisation LISTED in the site book (the instrument, its purpose sentence, its owner, its dependencies — the register being Chapter 2's collision-check input, the future admin's orientation, and the make-vs-take test's own audit: the customisation whose purpose sentence nobody can complete is a retirement candidate at the annual review, exactly as the roles and series were), and the register's health read honest: the customisation COUNT trended (the site accreting fields at pace has a make-vs-take discipline failing upstream — the count as the discipline's own metric, read at the walk), and the ownership current (the field whose owning function forgot it exists is debt with no creditor watching — reassigned or retired, never orphaned). The chapter's one-liner, for every implementation conversation: the best customisation is the one the standard way made unnecessary — and the certified admin earns more by preventing fields than by adding them.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Custom fields: the commonest change, fully governed
lessons.html:
When make wins the test, the commonest instrument is the custom field — small enough to seem casual, connected enough to deserve the full ceremony. The field chapter.

The field's anatomy, decided deliberately. Every property a policy: the LABEL (the human name — clear, the firm's vocabulary), the FIELDNAME (the technical name that lives FOREVER — set once, never casually: the fieldname is the identity every report, template, and script will reference, and the renamed fieldname breaks them all silently: the registrar law of module 3, at the field layer — named right at birth because rebirth is not offered), the TYPE (the data's shape — the select versus the free text being module 3's drift lesson pre-empted at design: the field that should be a governed list born as one, because the free-text field is the 'Lagos/lagos/LAGOS' factory), the PLACEMENT (the form's readability owned — the field landed in its logical section, not appended to the bottom of a form that becomes an archaeology of afterthoughts), and — the property this academy will not let be forgotten — the PERMISSION LEVEL (module 2's field-level fencing applying to new fields from birth: the custom field on a sensitive doctype DECIDED into its level deliberately — the pay-adjacent field born at the elevated level its content demands, because the field added at level 0 by default is the leak module 2's walk will find a year late: the tier design consulted at every field's birth, and the level noted in the register).

The behaviour options as policy. The field's rules, each an owner's decision: MANDATORY (the field that blocks saving — a process rule imposed on every user forever: set by the owning function's explicit choice, because the casual mandatory is the data-entry friction that breeds workarounds), DEFAULTS (the value pre-filled — convenience when right, silent error at scale when wrong: the default that stops being true keeps being filled), READ-ONLY and dependency conditions (the field's visibility and editability tied to the document's state — the behaviour layer used to make forms honest: the field that only matters when a condition holds, shown only then), and VALIDATION expectations routed properly (the rule beyond the field's own options — the cross-field check, the format enforcement — being the deeper end of the catalogue, engaged through the partner discipline when the need is real).

The downstream map. The field's connections, walked before creation because they are owned after: the IMPORT templates (module 3's fresh-template rule existing partly because fields change — the new field appearing in tomorrow's template, the load documentation updated), the REPORTS (the field created to be reported on actually added to the reports that need it — the field captured but never surfaced being effort without yield; the field surfaced in reports its viewers shouldn't see being module 2's report-leak, pre-empted), the PRINT formats where the field must appear (Chapter 5's coordination), and the FENCES (the level above, plus the field's interaction with the record-level territories where relevant). The chapter's procedure summary: the field request through the channel with its owner → the make-vs-take test → the anatomy decided property by property (level included, always) → the test-site build → the verification as the roles (the field present for those who should see it, ABSENT for those who shouldn't — the empirical habit at the field's birth) → production by the ceremony → the register's entry. Small instrument, full governance — because the field is small exactly once, at creation, and connected forever after.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Print formats: the document's face
lessons.html:
The print format is where the system meets the world: the invoice the customer holds, the payslip the worker files, the purchase order the supplier fulfils. The firm's outward face, governed accordingly. The formats chapter.

The format's standing. Why formats get their own chapter: the printed document is the EVIDENCE LAYER'S public half (the archives, disputes, and audits of six tracks hold PRINTED documents — the format is what they hold), the firm's brand in its counterparties' hands (the invoice that looks improvised prices the firm in its customers' minds — the letterhead, the layout, the completeness reading as competence exactly as the payslip-with-the-credit did), and the STATUTORY carrier (the invoice's tax content, the payslip's anatomy — the format is where the functions' legal requirements physically render, which makes format content a FUNCTION decision the admin implements: the invoice's tax lines confirmed by the accountant, the payslip's blocks per the payroll track's anatomy chapter, the statutory particulars per the adviser's reading — the admin owns the rendering; the functions own the rendered).

The format discipline. The governance, mapped to the ceremony: formats built and changed on the TEST SITE (the format is code-adjacent — the edit that breaks rendering breaks it for every user printing that doctype: rehearsed, always), VERIFIED against real documents (the format proven on the awkward cases, not the demo row — the long item list that paginates, the discount line, the zero-tax row, the credit note's negatives: the format that only works on pretty data fails at the counter's first ugly document), VERSIONED by the ceremony (the format's change logged — the before-copy retained so the rollback is a restore, not a rebuild: module 3's snapshot instinct at the format layer), and the DEFAULT governance explicit (which format prints by default per doctype, who may choose alternates — the format selection being a small permission with a large face: the draft-watermarked internal format on a customer's invoice is a governance miss the defaults prevent).

The sealed-data law. The format's deepest rule, inherited from six tracks: the format renders the DOCUMENT'S data — it does not improve it (the format that 'fixes' a value in rendering — the rounded total, the relabeled line, the hidden inconvenient field — has created a second version of a sealed document: the printed invoice disagreeing with the stored invoice is the one-version law broken at the layer the counterparty holds, and the dispute where the customer's paper contradicts the system's record is the exact scenario the law exists to prevent), with the corollary for changes: the format change applies to future prints of any document, so the REPRINT of a sealed document must render faithfully what was sealed (the archive's integrity extending to its printed face — the payslip reprinted for the visa file matching the payslip issued, per module 4 of the payroll track's reissued-slip conviction: this chapter is where that conviction gets its machinery).

The format inventory. The register's format page: every active format per doctype listed (its purpose, its owner-function, its default status, its last change), the retired formats disabled rather than deleted (the museum discipline — the old format may need to render an old document's reprint faithfully), and the annual review beside the customisation register's (the format nobody prints retired; the format whose statutory content aged — the reform that changed the invoice's requirements — flagged to its owning function at the pre-season reviews the functions already run: the format inventory joining the compliance calendar where the content is compliance). The chapter's closing frame: the print format is the only part of the system most counterparties will ever see — and the certified admin treats it with the care that fact deserves: function-owned content, ceremony-governed changes, awkward-case verification, and a face that never contradicts the record behind it.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Workflows & automation: authority as configuration
lessons.html:
The approval chains, notification rules, and automations — the layer where six tracks' separations physically live, changed with the care that fact demands. The automation chapter.

Workflows: the separations, materialised. The recognition first: the WORKFLOW definitions are where the academy's authority designs run — the document's states and transitions (draft → submitted for approval → approved → sealed), WHO may move each transition (the roles at each gate — the preparer-approver separations of the payroll run, the two-names patterns of the money tracks, the requisition approvals of procurement: every one a workflow rule or a submit-permission, which module 2 taught as configuration and this chapter teaches as CHANGEABLE configuration), and the consequence stated plainly: a workflow change is an authority change — the transition's role edited is a separation redrawn, decided by the owning function's named authority exactly as a mandate change would be (the workflow edit that 'streamlines' an approval out of existence has repealed a control some track built deliberately — the admin who receives that request routes it to the control's owner with the design's reason attached, because the streamlining request is sometimes right and the deciding is never the admin's).

The workflow change's special cares. Beyond the standard ceremony, the layer's own checks: the IN-FLIGHT documents considered (the live documents mid-workflow when the definition changes — the change tested against them on the test site: the edit that orphans forty pending approvals in an unreachable state is this layer's classic break, caught in rehearsal), the STATE-permission interaction verified (module 2's union-filter-state model — the workflow's states and the roles' rights proven together, as the roles), and the audit face preserved (the workflow's history on documents — who approved what, when — being evidence the functions rely on: the change that would blur past approvals weighed against that evidence's standing).

Notifications & auto-communication. The rules that make the system speak: the NOTIFICATION rules (the alert on the event — the approval waiting, the threshold crossed, the expiry approaching: the reminder engines every track's calendar relies on, administered here and TESTED per the HR track's dummy-certificate discipline — the notification that silently stopped is the calendar's silent failure, and the periodic test-fire is its detector), the AUTO-EMAIL rules (the document dispatched on the event — the invoice to the customer, the slip released with the credit: the payroll track's choreography having a rule behind it, owned and verified), and the FLOOD governance (the notification volume read deliberately — the users drowning in alerts stop reading alerts, which un-builds every reminder the calendars depend on: the notification set pruned to the actionable, per the owning functions' choices — the quiet, relevant notification stream being a designed artifact, not a default).

Assignment & scheduling rules. The remaining automation briefly and completely: the ASSIGNMENT rules (the document routed to its owner automatically — the request channel's own queue running on one), the SCHEDULED automations (the recurring documents, the auto-generated entries — each a standing decision reviewed annually: the automation that outlives its reason generates artifacts nobody reads, the museum discipline at the automation layer), and the shared law across all of it, closing the chapter: automation is AUTHORITY EXERCISED REPEATEDLY — the rule that fires a hundred times a month is a decision made a hundred times a month, which is exactly why its creation deserves the full ceremony and its owner's name: the automation register beside the customisation register, every rule with its purpose sentence, its owner, and its last test-fire date — the system that speaks and routes by itself, governed like the staff member it effectively is.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The change ceremony: one procedure for everything
lessons.html:
The module's instruments assembled into its single procedure: the CHANGE CEREMONY — every change, both streams, one shape. The procedure chapter.

The ceremony's steps. Walked once, applied always: 1 — the REQUEST (through module 1's channel, with the owning function named — the change begins as a document, like everything in this academy), 2 — the DECISION (the make-vs-take test where it applies; the owner's authorisation always — the admin executes decisions, never makes the functions'), 3 — the DESIGN NOTE (what will change, why, the expected effect, the affected flows — a paragraph, not a thesis: the note's job is that the verification has a target and the log has a story), 4 — the REHEARSAL (the test site, refreshed recently enough to rehearse honestly — the change built and proven there: nothing first in production, the module's spine), 5 — the WINDOW (the change landed in the quiet hour, scheduled against the firm's calendar — the format rebuilt during the counter's rush is self-inflicted downtime), 6 — the EXECUTION (the change applied to production exactly as rehearsed — the 'small improvement while I'm in here' refused: the ceremony covers what it covers, and the drive-by addition is an unceremonied change hiding inside a ceremonied one), 7 — the VERIFICATION (the affected flows walked AS THE ROLES — the empirical habit: the change proven present, correct, and non-leaking on production, per the design note's targets), and 8 — the LOG (below).

The change log entry. The ceremony's permanent residue, its fields fixed: WHAT changed (the instrument and its specifics), WHY (the request and its owner), WHO executed, WHEN, the VERIFICATION's result, and — the field that makes the log a safety system rather than a diary — HOW TO REVERSE (the rollback path recorded while it is obvious: the before-copy's location, the field's removal steps, the format version to restore — the reversibility clause of the module's law, cashed as a log field: the change whose reversal requires archaeology was never reversible in any sense that matters at 8 a.m. on the bad morning).

The rollback readiness. The ceremony's insurance layer: the BEFORE-STATE captured per instrument (the format's copy, the field's specification, the workflow's export, module 3's snapshot for data-touching changes — the capture proportional to the instrument, always cheap, occasionally priceless), the rollback REHEARSED for the consequential change (the big change's undo proven on test alongside its do — the reversal that was never tried is module 4's untested backup wearing a different hat), and the rollback DECISION pre-named (who calls it, on what evidence, inside what window — the change that is failing in production needs its retreat decided in minutes, and the pre-named authority is the difference between a rollback and a debate).

The ceremony's proportionality. The honest sizing, closing the chapter: the ceremony SCALES (the label typo fixed with a two-line log entry and a glance; the workflow redesign with the full eight steps and a rehearsed rollback — the judgment being the certified admin's craft, with the floor absolute: even the smallest change gets its log line, because the drift of Chapter 1 is made of changes that were each too small to log), and the ceremony's cost restated as the module's economics: minutes per change, against the archaeology site and the counter-morning break — the fifth law being, like every law before it, the cheap discipline that makes the expensive disaster structurally unavailable.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's change year
lessons.html:
Both streams, one ceremony, twelve months. Every chapter clocks in.

The update stream (Ch. 2). The receiving ritual installs: the announcement channel routed to the admin's watched queue, the update calendar cross-checked against the firm's (one maintenance window successfully moved off payroll-run week through the boundary conversation — asked, and answered: the firm that never asks never benefits, proven), and the post-update walk's checklist drawn from the firm's real critical paths. The year's major platform update delivers the chapter's classic: the dawn walk catches a shifted column layout in a stock report the Ibadan branch reads every morning — flagged to Inventory's owner and repaired before the branch opens (the break that would have been a support-ticket morning caught by fifteen minutes of deliberate walking), and the release notes' triage flags one deprecation touching a custom format — the collision fixed in preview week, not production morning.

The firm's stream (Ch. 3-4). The make-vs-take test earns its chapter in month two: Selling requests a custom 'customer priority' field — the test walks it and finds a PROCESS gap wearing a field (the request is really an ungoverned follow-up flow wanting the standing machinery) — the customisation REFUSED with the routing that makes refusal constructive, and the process fixed at the process layer through Selling's own design (the best customisation is the one the standard way made unnecessary — the register's note quotes the chapter). The year's one genuine field lands by full ceremony: a regulatory-reference field on the supplier doctype (Procurement's real gap, the test passed) — anatomy decided property by property, the fieldname set for forever, and the PERMISSION LEVEL decided at birth (the field placed at the elevated level its content warranted — the module-2 walk finding nothing a year later because there was nothing to find: the leak pre-empted at the moment of creation, exactly as designed).

The face and the authority (Ch. 5-6). The invoice format is rebuilt in quarter two: content confirmed line by line with the accountant (the tax lines per the current reading — the function owning the rendered, the admin the rendering), rehearsed against the awkward cases (the long-list pagination catching a footer collision on test — the ugly-document verification doing its one job), versioned with its before-copy, and defaulted by the ceremony. One workflow change travels the year: Selling's owner redraws a discount-approval threshold — routed as the authority change it is (the owner decides; the design note names the separation being adjusted), tested against in-flight documents on rehearsal (two pending approvals verified to survive the transition), verified as the roles. And one notification prune lands in quarter three: the flood read finds users ignoring a twelve-alert daily stream — pruned to four actionable rules with the owning functions, and the reminder engines' quarterly test-fire calendar established (the dummy-expiry test of the HR track, adopted as the platform's own rhythm).

The log at year end (Ch. 7). The change log's twelfth month reads as the module intends: thirty-one entries — two platform updates with their walks, one field, one format rebuild, one workflow change, one refusal (logged deliberately: the road not taken is part of the site's story), one notification prune, and twenty-four small ceremonied changes each with its how-to-reverse line. One rollback exercised in anger (a report tweak that slowed a heavy screen — reversed in four minutes by its own log entry's path, the pre-named decision working as written). The ops lead's year-note closes the case: a year ago every change was a small gamble we mostly won. Now every change is a rehearsal we already watched succeed — and the one that failed was undone before anyone finished complaining about it.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the fifth law
lessons.html:
The change layer's scar tissue. Symptom → disease → fix.

Pattern 1 — the untested update. Symptom: the platform update discovered by the counter; the shifted report found by the branch that reads it; the break's first detector a support ticket. Disease: the host's stream received passively (Ch. 2). Fix: the receiving ritual — notes triaged, previews used, the post-update walk at dawn, findings routed before opening.

Pattern 2 — customisation sprawl. Symptom: the site accreting fields at pace; forms as archaeologies of afterthoughts; every update a collision lottery; nobody able to say why half of it exists. Disease: make-vs-take never run (Ch. 3). Fix: the test on every request, the register with purpose sentences and owners, the count trended, and the annual retirement of the unexplainable.

Pattern 3 — the level-0 leak. Symptom: the sensitive custom field visible to every role that opens the record; the tier design defeated by a default nobody decided. Disease: the permission level unconsidered at the field's birth (Ch. 4). Fix: the level as a mandatory birth decision — the tier design consulted, the level in the register, the verification as the roles before production.

Pattern 4 — the format that improves the data. Symptom: the printed invoice disagreeing with the stored one; the reprint that contradicts the original; the dispute where the customer's paper beats the system's record. Disease: the one-version law broken at the rendering layer (Ch. 5). Fix: the sealed-data law — the format renders faithfully, reprints match issues, and format changes never rewrite the archive's face.

Pattern 5 — the workflow edited live. Symptom: approvals orphaned mid-flight; a separation quietly repealed; the control some track built streamlined out of existence by a helpful edit. Disease: authority changed without its owner, on production, untested (Ch. 6). Fix: the workflow change as an authority change — the owner decides, the in-flight documents rehearsed, the roles verified, the design's reason attached to every streamlining request.

Pattern 6 — the changes nobody remembers. Symptom: 'when did this start?' unanswerable; the baseline unknown; every debug an excavation; the new admin inheriting a mystery. Disease: the log never kept (Ch. 1, 7) — the drift made of changes each too small to record. Fix: the ceremony's absolute floor — every change its log line, every consequential change its how-to-reverse — the site's story readable, forever.

The fifth law. The custodian, the fences, the masters, the survival — and now the evolution governed: every change is staged, documented, and reversible — the host's stream received by ritual, the firm's stream gated by make-vs-take, fields born with their levels, formats that never contradict their records, workflow edits as the authority changes they are, and one ceremony whose log tells the site's whole story with the way back written beside every step forward. The site that changes this way improves for years without accumulating mysteries — and the certified admin is why. Module 6 turns to the system's connections: printing's siblings — email, notifications at the boundary, and the integration inventory.

email_integrations.title: Sysadmin 6 — Printing, Email & Integrations
email_integrations.desc: Every message and integration has an owner: the email machinery with firm-domain identity and custodied credentials, the queue as the outbound ledger, the communication map with recipient hygiene, the integration inventory with the build boundary, API key custody with rotation by events, and designed failure modes with monthly reconciliation where money and statute flow.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The system speaks and connects: every channel owned
lessons.html:
The site does not only store and compute — it SPEAKS (the invoice emailed, the slip released, the reminder fired, the document printed) and it CONNECTS (the SMS gateway, the payment confirmation, the statutory e-invoicing endpoint, the partner-built bridges). Every one of those surfaces carries the firm's name, the firm's data, or the firm's legal obligations into the world — and the module's thesis is the track's sixth law forming: every message and every integration has an owner — because the unowned channel fails silently, leaks quietly, and embarrasses publicly.

The two surface families. The module's map: the OUTBOUND surfaces (Chapters 2-4 — the email machinery, its deliverability and queue, and the communication map of everything the system sends: the printed document's operational life included, its design having been Chapter 5 of the change module — this module owns the SENDING, the previous owned the shape), and the CONNECTED surfaces (Chapters 5-7 — the integrations' inventory, their credentials' custody, and their failure modes: the doors in the site's walls, each one deliberate, documented, and watched). The families share the module's one discipline, previewed: each channel carries a NAME (the function that owns its content and its consequences — the invoice email is selling's channel; the statutory connection is the accountant's; the admin custodians the plumbing of all of them, per the split now seven modules old), a MAP entry (the site book's communication and integration pages — Chapters 4 and 5's deliverables), and a FAILURE ANSWER (what happens when it stops — designed in calm, per module 4's whole philosophy, because the channel's failure mode chosen in advance is a degraded mode, and the one discovered live is an incident).

The unowned channel, convicted in advance. The diseases this module prevents, named as its opening indictment: the invoice that stopped sending in March and nobody noticed until the debtors' calls (the unread queue — Chapter 3), the payslip emailed to a stale address (the recipient hygiene breach — Chapter 4, with the payroll track's tightest tier bleeding through a typo), the credential pasted in a group chat and never rotated after the leaver (Chapter 6 — the key to the firm's SMS identity or worse, walking out the door in someone's chat history), the integration that a departed consultant built and nobody can name (the orphaned door — Chapter 5), and the statutory connection whose rejected submissions accumulate unread (Chapter 7 — the compliance channel failing in a queue nobody owns, which is the unremitted-month disease of the payroll track wearing an API's clothes). Each disease is an ownership absence — and the module's cure, chapter by chapter, is the register that makes every channel answer to a name.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The email machinery: accounts, identity & custody
lessons.html:
The system's voice begins with its email accounts — the machinery that determines whether the firm's messages arrive, from whom they appear to come, and who controls the voice. The accounts chapter.

The outgoing account. The sender, governed: the system sends through a configured OUTGOING account — and the first discipline is IDENTITY: the firm's documents sent from the FIRM'S domain address (the invoices from the firm's billing identity, not from anyone's personal mailbox — the personal-address sender being Chapter 9's opening disease: the firm whose invoices arrive from a staff member's private account has coupled its billing voice to one person's employment, mixed its evidence trail into a private mailbox it cannot search or retain, and taught its customers to trust a sender the firm does not control: the identity fixed as the module's first act at every implementation), the account's shape decided deliberately (the single firm voice versus the purpose addresses — the billing address, the payroll's notifications, the support inbox: few, named, and mapped — each a communication-map entry, not a proliferation), and the DELIVERABILITY foundations confirmed at boundary altitude (the domain's authentication records — the signatures that tell receiving servers the firm's mail is genuinely the firm's — confirmed with the domain's custodian and the host through the boundary conversation: the admin does not administer the records; the admin verifies the answer is yes and files it in the site book, because the unauthenticated domain's mail lands in spam folders, and the firm's invoices in spam is a collections problem wearing a technical costume).

The incoming accounts. Where the system LISTENS: the inbound account pulling a mailbox into the system (the support address becoming tickets, the documents channel receiving — legitimate, powerful, and each one a door: the inbound account's scope decided — what it creates, who triages it — and its own hygiene watched: the inbox-to-system bridge that creates records from whatever arrives is an import door in disguise, and module 3's governance instincts apply), with the unused kept closed (the fewer listening doors, the smaller the surface — the minimalism of module 2's least-privilege, applied to mailboxes).

The account custody. The credentials' governance, joining module 2's lifecycle: the email accounts' credentials held in the firm's custody (the password known to the CUSTODY, not to a person's memory alone — stored per Chapter 6's credential disciplines), the shared-purpose mailbox governed (the billing address read by the role, its access granted and revoked by the same events as everything else — the mailbox being a resource like any other, on the access register), and the ROTATION events wired (the leaver who knew the account's credentials triggers its rotation — HR 7's checklist and module 2's lifecycle both pointing at this desk: the separation that disables the user but leaves the shared mailbox's password unchanged has closed the front door and left the side window open, and the module's custody register makes the side windows enumerable). The chapter's summary for the site book: few accounts, firm-domain identity, authenticated delivery, custodied credentials, rotation by events — the voice owned before a single message is judged.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Deliverability & the queue: the outbound ledger
lessons.html:
Every message the system sends passes through the EMAIL QUEUE — which makes the queue the outbound ledger: the complete, timestamped record of what the firm's system said, to whom, and whether it arrived. Read accordingly. The queue chapter.

The queue as ledger. The reframe that organises the chapter: the queue is not plumbing to ignore but a REGISTER to read — every outbound message a row with a state (queued, sent, failed), which gives the admin two things the academy prizes: the EVIDENCE function (the dispute's 'we never received the invoice' answered by pointing — the queue's sent record with its timestamp and recipient being the outbound half of the evidence layer, filed beside the document it carried: the answered-by-pointing law extended to the sending itself) and the HEALTH function (the queue's shape read on the daily glance — module 1's posture now given its email column: the failure count, the stuck messages, the volume anomaly).

The failure read. The failed message triaged by its kind: the BOUNCE (the recipient address dead or wrong — routed to the CONTACT'S owner for correction, because the bounce is a master-data finding wearing an email costume: the customer's stale address fixed in the customer record by selling's pen, per module 3's custodianship — the admin routes; the function corrects), the REJECTION (the receiving server refusing — the deliverability signal read: the pattern of rejections at one domain is a conversation; the pattern everywhere is the authentication check of Chapter 2 re-run), the STUCK message (the queue jammed — the background machinery's health, module 7's terrain, glanced daily exactly because the silent jam is the invoice-that-never-sent disease incubating), and the RETRY discipline honest (the transient failure retried by the machinery; the permanent failure CLOSED with its cause — the queue that accumulates ancient failures unread is the unread queue of Chapter 1's indictment: triaged to zero on its rhythm, like every worked list in this academy).

The spam reality. The deliverability hygiene, at the admin's altitude: the firm's mail lands where the receiving world decides — and the admin's levers are the foundations (Chapter 2's authentication, confirmed), the CONTENT discipline (the outbound templates professional and consistent — the all-caps urgent subject line is a spam signal the firm sends about itself), the VOLUME shape (the sudden bulk blast from a transactional address teaches receiving servers suspicion — the mass communication need served deliberately, not improvised through the invoice channel), and the FEEDBACK read (the customers who report 'it went to spam' being a signal logged and investigated, not shrugged at — the firm's deliverability being a reputation maintained by hygiene, exactly as its trade reputation is).

The evidence discipline. The chapter's closing tie to six tracks: the sent-record RETAINED per the evidence horizons (the queue's history and the communication log kept per the retention conversations of module 4 — the 'was it sent?' question answerable for as long as the dispute horizon runs), and the sending's provenance clean (the message sent by the system, from the governed account, logged in the queue — versus the document downloaded and forwarded from personal mailboxes, which exits the evidence layer entirely: the staff habit of personal forwarding read as the workaround signal it is, and the governed send made easier than the workaround, per the academy's oldest adoption law).

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The communication map: what the system sends, to whom
lessons.html:
The module's first register: the COMMUNICATION MAP — every stream the system sends, on one page, each with its owner. The map chapter.

The map's rows. The outbound inventory, drawn from six tracks' choreographies: the INVOICES and statements to customers (selling's channel — the trigger, the template, the sender identity, the attachment's format), the PURCHASE orders to suppliers (procurement's), the PAYSLIPS to staff (payroll's — with its special standing below), the REMINDERS and notifications (the expiry alerts, the approval nudges, the calendar's engine — each rule from module 5's automation register cross-referenced here by its audience), the RECEIPTS and confirmations (the payment acknowledged, the order confirmed), and the STATUTORY dispatches where the functions use them — each row carrying the same columns: WHAT goes out, TRIGGERED by what, TO whom, FROM which account, OWNED by which function, and last VERIFIED when (the map being the site book's page that answers, in one look, the question every new admin and every auditor asks: what does this system say to the world, and on whose authority?).

The recipient hygiene. The map's data-quality dependency, stated with module weight: every stream is aimed by CONTACT DATA (the customer's email on the customer master, the employee's address on the employee record) — which makes recipient quality a master-data discipline with a confidentiality edge: the WRONG-RECIPIENT dispatch being this chapter's central disaster (the payslip to a stale address is the payroll track's tightest tier breached by a typo; the customer statement to the wrong customer is two relationships damaged in one send), and the hygiene mechanised: the sensitive streams' recipients verified on their events (the joiner's address confirmed at onboarding; the change-of-address event updating the master BEFORE the next cycle — HR's events feeding the map's aim), the bounce loop closing corrections fast (Chapter 3's routing), and the highest-sensitivity streams DOUBLE-KEYED (the payslip channel's recipient source read from the governed master only — never a manually-maintained side list, because the side list is where stale addresses live: the one-version law aiming the most dangerous mail).

The sensitive streams' standing. The map's tiers, honest: not all streams are equal — the payslip and anything pay-adjacent carries module 2's tightest-tier weight IN TRANSIT (the delivery choices the payroll track designed — the attachment protections, the self-service pull versus the push — administered here as configuration, with the admin's conduct rule explicit: the admin who can see the queue does not open the payslip attachments passing through it — the custodian-not-owner law at the mail bag: the postman's ethics, enforced by module 8's conduct standard and its logs), and the statutory streams carrying legal weight (the dispatch that discharges an obligation — its proof-of-send retained per the adviser's horizons).

The map's maintenance. The register's life: updated by the ceremony (every new stream or changed template through module 5's change process, the map's row updated in the same act), verified on the walk (the annual re-verification — each stream test-fired or evidenced live within the year: the stream that hasn't demonstrably fired in a year is either dead weight or a silent failure, and the walk decides which), and read at every incident ('what does the system send?' being the first question of half the module's diagnoses — answered by the page, in seconds, which is the entire reason the page exists).

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Integrations: the inventory & the boundary
lessons.html:
The connected surfaces: the doors in the site's walls where other systems reach in and the firm's data reaches out. Every door deliberate, documented, and owned. The inventory chapter.

What the doors are. The trade-scale integration landscape, named honestly: the PAYMENT rails (the gateway confirmations, the bank-adjacent feeds — money's arrival told to the system by machines), the MESSAGING gateways (the SMS and messaging channels the notifications ride — the delivery confirmations, the customer alerts), the STATUTORY connections (the e-invoicing and compliance endpoints where the regulator's machinery receives the firm's documents — the connection where an API failure is a COMPLIANCE event, given its own weight in Chapter 7), the PARTNER bridges (the connections the implementation partner built — the custom flows, the external tools), and the INBOUND doors (the webhooks and endpoints where outside events arrive — each one a listening surface with Chapter 6's verification duties). The chapter's frame for all of them: an integration is a STANDING RELATIONSHIP between systems — it has a purpose, a counterparty, credentials, a data flow, and a failure mode, exactly like a supplier relationship has terms, contacts, and risks — and it is governed like one: on a register, with an owner, reviewed on a rhythm.

The integration inventory. The register's columns, fixed: each integration's PURPOSE (one sentence — the connection that cannot be described joins the retirement candidates, per the standing catalogue law), its OWNING FUNCTION (the payment confirmation is treasury's; the statutory endpoint the accountant's; the SMS gateway owned by whoever owns its messages' content — the admin custodians plumbing, never consequences), its COUNTERPARTY and support path (the provider, the contact, the escalation — the boundary map's pattern per connection), its CREDENTIALS' custody entry (Chapter 6's register cross-referenced), its DATA FLOW (what crosses, in which direction, how sensitive — the flow's tier read against module 2's designs: the integration that exports pay-adjacent data is a tightest-tier door and audited as one), its FAILURE MODE (Chapter 7's designed answer), and its last REVIEW date.

The build boundary. Who makes the doors: integrations are BUILT through the implementation partner's discipline (the deep end of module 5's catalogue — the connection's construction, its error handling, its mapping logic being engineering the site admin commissions, not improvises: the admin's role in the build being the REQUIREMENTS side — the purpose, the owner, the data flow, the failure mode specified — and the acceptance side — the integration proven on test, the inventory's row completed, before production), and OPERATED by the admin thereafter (the monitoring, the credential rotations, the review rhythm — the custody handed over WITH documentation, because the partner-built door whose workings left with the partner is the orphaned integration of Chapter 1's indictment: the acceptance checklist includes the door's own runbook, or the acceptance is not complete). The chapter's closing rule, the module's law in inventory form: no door without a row; no row without an owner; no owner without a failure answer — the site whose connections all answer to names is the site where 'what is this connection?' is never asked in an incident for the first time.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Credentials & API custody: the keys to the firm
lessons.html:
Every integration, account, and automated connection runs on CREDENTIALS — the API keys, tokens, and passwords that ARE the firm's identity to machines. Held accordingly. The custody chapter.

What a credential is. The weight set first: the API key is not a password-like inconvenience — it IS the firm, to every system that accepts it (the key to the SMS gateway can speak to customers AS the firm; the statutory connection's credentials can file AS the firm; the payment rail's token can read money's movements — each credential a signature stamp, and the academy's oldest custody instincts applying at full strength: the cheque-signing disciplines of the money tracks, at the machine layer), which sets the custody bar: credentials are held the way the firm holds its most consequential keys — enumerated, stored properly, issued narrowly, rotated on events, and never, ever ambient.

The storage law. The disciplines, plainly: credentials live in GOVERNED storage (the credential store or sealed register the firm designates — access-controlled per module 2, its readers enumerable), and never in the ambient places the trade actually keeps them (the group chat where the key was pasted 'temporarily' three years ago — the chat history being a credential store with no access control, no rotation, and no leaver process; the spreadsheet named passwords.xlsx; the sticky note; the one person's memory — each an ambient copy the firm cannot enumerate, which means cannot rotate, which means does not control), with the module's honest note about the trade's reality: the cleanup engagement's credential audit always finds the ambient copies, and the certified admin's first custody act is the ENUMERATION (every credential found, listed, and re-homed) followed by the ROTATION (every credential whose ambient history is unknowable rotated on principle — the key that lived in a chat is treated as leaked because its readership is unknowable, which is the conservative instinct every custody track taught).

The issuance disciplines. The keys' lifecycle, mirroring module 2's: ONE credential per connection (the shared key serving three integrations cannot be rotated for one without breaking two, and cannot be revoked for a compromised door without closing the innocent ones — the per-door key being the blast-radius discipline at the credential layer), scoped NARROWLY (the key issued with the least capability the connection needs — the read-only feed holding a read-only token: least privilege for machines, exactly as for humans), ROTATED on events (the leaver who knew or could know a credential triggers its rotation — module 2's lifecycle and HR 7's checklist both landing here: the credential register's rotation column making the leaver-event's credential sweep a checklist line instead of a guess; plus the calendar rotation for the long-lived keys the events never touched), and RETIRED with their doors (the integration decommissioned has its credentials revoked in the same ceremony — the dead door with a live key being an entrance nobody watches).

The key register & webhook hygiene. The chapter's deliverables: the CREDENTIAL REGISTER (every key: what it opens, what it can do, where it is stored, who may access it, when last rotated — the register that makes the leaver sweep, the audit answer, and the incident response each a lookup), and the INBOUND door's verification (the webhook that receives outside events VERIFIES its callers — the endpoint that believes whatever arrives is an open gate for forged events: the verification's presence confirmed at acceptance, per Chapter 5's checklist, because the listening door's hygiene is part of the door). The chapter's closing sentence, for the site book's custody page: a credential is the firm's signature in a machine's hands — enumerated, stored, scoped, rotated, retired: the five verbs that separate custody from exposure.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Integration health: designed failure & the reconciliation instinct
lessons.html:
Every door will fail — the gateway down, the endpoint rejecting, the confirmation lagging. The difference between an incident and a degraded mode is whether the failure was DESIGNED. The health chapter.

The designed failure mode. The inventory's hardest column, completed per door: for each integration, the answer to 'what happens when it stops?' written in calm — the SMS gateway down (the notifications queue and retry? fall silent? — decided: the critical alerts carrying a fallback channel per the continuity instincts of module 4, the routine ones waiting), the PAYMENT confirmation lagging (the money's arrival told late — the receipt process's manual verification path standing, per the money tracks' own disciplines: the integration ACCELERATES the confirmation, it does not replace the reconciliation), and the STATUTORY endpoint rejecting or unreachable (the weightiest door's failure — the submission that cannot land does not suspend the obligation: the failure mode here includes the DEADLINE awareness (the retry window against the statutory clock), the rejection queue's triage (below), and the escalation to the owning function while time remains — the compliance door's outage being a calendar event, not just a technical one).

The rejection queue, owned. The chapter's central discipline, weighted for the statutory doors: the integration that submits documents accumulates a REJECTION stream (the invoice the endpoint refused — the validation failure, the mismatched particulars, the schema drift after an update) — and the stream is a WORKED LIST with an owner (triaged on its rhythm to zero, each rejection corrected at its source and resubmitted — the rejected statutory submission being a compliance document in limbo, and the queue nobody reads being Chapter 1's gravest indictment: the firm that believes it is compliant because the system 'sends automatically' while rejections accumulate unread has automated its way into the unremitted-month disease with better technology), the rejection PATTERNS read (the cluster of one failure kind is a master-data or configuration finding routed per module 3 — the rejections as the endpoint's own quality feedback), and the queue's health on the glance (module 7 of this track formalises the read; this chapter establishes the duty).

The reconciliation instinct. The trio discipline of the payroll track, generalised to every door where money or statute flows: the integration's records reconciled against the system's on a rhythm — the gateway's delivery report against the sent register (the messages the firm paid for matching the messages the system dispatched), the payment rail's settlement report against the receipts entered (the money the machines announced matching the money the books recorded — the money tracks' bank reconciliation extended to its feeder), and the statutory endpoint's ACCEPTED register against the firm's issued documents (the compliance door's reconciliation being the one that catches the silent gap: the documents issued minus the documents accepted equals the rejection queue plus the never-submitted — an equation read monthly, because its non-zero answer is a finding with a deadline), each reconciliation owned by the door's owning function with the admin providing the machinery — the split, one last time.

The review rhythm. The doors' calendar: the integration REVIEW annually per door (the purpose still true, the volume read, the credentials' rotation current, the failure mode still correct, the counterparty relationship live — the door re-justified or retired: the museum discipline at the connection layer), the acceptance re-run after major changes (the platform update that touches an integration's terrain triggers its verification — module 5's collision check, cashed), and the incident learning loop (the door that failed teaches its runbook — the post-incident amendment, per module 4's pattern). The chapter's one-liner: doors fail; owned doors fail gracefully — designed modes, worked rejection queues, monthly reconciliations, and an annual look that asks each door to justify its hinges.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's connected year
lessons.html:
The voice and the doors, governed through a year. Every chapter clocks in.

The voice fixed (Ch. 2-3). The email overhaul opens the year: the audit finds the classic — invoices sending from the accountant's personal address ('it was set up that way at go-live and worked, so nobody touched it') — the sender identity moved to the firm's billing address, the domain's authentication confirmed with the host in one boundary ticket, and the deliverability difference measurable within a month (two customers who 'never got invoices' start getting them — the spam folder's tax, refunded). The queue read enters the daily glance and pays for itself in week three: a stuck-queue jam caught at 7 a.m. (a configuration hiccup after a mail-provider change) — cleared before the day's statements went out late, the invoice-that-never-sent disease caught in its incubation.

The map and the near-miss (Ch. 4). The communication map's first draft lists eleven streams — and its recipient-hygiene pass delivers the chapter's sober moment: the payslip channel found reading addresses from a hand-maintained list predating the HR track's master (the side list three addresses stale — one belonging to a LEAVER: the payslip that would have gone to a departed employee's inbox, caught by the map's double-key rule before the next run instead of by the breach after it). The channel re-pointed to the governed master the same week; the side list deleted; the finding logged with the severity it deserved — and the MD's note enters the site book: we nearly posted a payslip through a dead man's letterbox. The map earns its page.

The doors inventoried (Ch. 5-6). The integration inventory's first census finds four doors: the SMS gateway (notifications and delivery alerts), the statutory e-invoicing connection (the accountant's door), a payment-confirmation feed, and one ORPHAN — a bridge built by a departed consultant during implementation, purpose unknown, still holding live credentials. The orphan's investigation (the partner consulted, the data flow read) finds it long-dead in function — decommissioned by ceremony, its credentials revoked (the dead door's live key, closed). The credential enumeration re-homes every key from its ambient places (two from a WhatsApp thread, one from a drawer notebook — each rotated on the leaked-until-proven-otherwise principle), and the register's rotation column meets its first leaver event in month seven: the checklist's credential sweep rotating the two keys the departing supervisor's role could reach — a checklist line, not a guess, exactly as designed.

The failures, designed and met (Ch. 7). The failure modes written in quarter one are used twice: the SMS gateway's regional outage in month five runs its designed mode (critical expiry alerts re-routed to the fallback channel, routine notifications queued — no incident, a degraded Tuesday), and the statutory door delivers the year's compliance catch: the monthly issued-minus-accepted reconciliation finds a non-zero answer — a batch of rejections accumulated after a schema update (a particulars mismatch the automatic sender never announced) — triaged to zero inside the deadline window, the root cause fixed at the master (module 3's routing), and the reconciliation's monthly seat vindicated in one read: the firm that would have discovered the gap in a penalty letter discovered it in its own equation. The ops lead's year-note closes the case: every message now has a sender we own, and every door has a name on it. The system talks to the world like a firm, not like a hobby.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the sixth law
lessons.html:
The connected layer's scar tissue. Symptom → disease → fix.

Pattern 1 — the personal-address sender. Symptom: invoices from a staff member's private mailbox; the evidence trail in an account the firm cannot search; the billing voice coupled to one person's employment. Disease: identity never governed (Ch. 2). Fix: firm-domain sender identities, few and mapped; authentication confirmed; the voice owned before a message is judged.

Pattern 2 — the unread queue. Symptom: the invoice that stopped sending in March, discovered by the debtors' calls in June; failures accumulating unread; the outbound ledger treated as plumbing. Disease: the queue never made a register (Ch. 3). Fix: the daily glance's email column, failures triaged by kind to zero, bounces routed to the contact's owner, the sent-record retained as evidence.

Pattern 3 — the stale-recipient breach. Symptom: the payslip to a departed employee's inbox; the statement to the wrong customer; the tightest tier defeated by a typo. Disease: recipient data ungoverned, side lists live (Ch. 4). Fix: sensitive streams aimed from the governed master only, addresses verified on their events, the bounce loop closing corrections fast.

Pattern 4 — the credential in the group chat. Symptom: keys pasted 'temporarily' years ago; readership unknowable; the leaver's chat history a credential store; rotation never. Disease: ambient custody (Ch. 6). Fix: enumeration, governed storage, one key per door, narrow scopes, rotation by events and calendar — leaked-until-proven-otherwise for every ambient survivor.

Pattern 5 — the orphaned integration. Symptom: the door a departed consultant built; purpose unknown, credentials live, workings undocumented; 'what is this connection?' asked for the first time in an incident. Disease: acceptance without custody (Ch. 5). Fix: the inventory — no door without a row, no row without an owner — the build boundary's acceptance checklist including the door's own runbook, and the orphans decommissioned by ceremony.

Pattern 6 — the unreconciled compliance door. Symptom: rejections accumulating in a queue nobody owns; 'the system sends automatically' mistaken for 'we are compliant'; the gap discovered in a penalty letter. Disease: automation trusted without reconciliation (Ch. 7). Fix: the rejection queue as a worked list with a deadline-aware owner, and the monthly equation — issued minus accepted equals rejections plus never-submitted — read to zero.

The sixth law. The custodian, the fences, the masters, the survival, the evolution — and now the voice and the doors: every message and every integration has an owner — the firm's voice sent from identities it controls through a queue read as a ledger, every stream mapped and aimed from governed masters, every door on an inventory with custodied keys and a designed failure, and every money- or statute-bearing connection reconciled monthly to zero. The system that speaks and connects this way faces the world like a firm — and the certified admin is why. Module 7 turns inward: monitoring, performance, and the health reads that let the admin know before anyone feels.
